docs.title: Debrief v4
docs.text:
Debrief helps analysts turn the record of an exercise or deployment into understanding: reconstructing tracks, measuring geometry, annotating what happened, and producing reports whose every figure traces back to its data.

Debrief v4 replaces the 25-year-old Eclipse application with one shared core that every community uses: a VS Code extension, analysis tools written in Python, and plots stored as plain GeoJSON in STAC catalogues with their provenance inside.

  • Blog: short posts as each capability lands.
  • Guides: the style guide, interaction models and tool-author guide that keep Debrief consistent as it grows.

Development happens in the open at debrief/fuudee. Everything on this site uses unclassified sample data only.

docs.title: Try Debrief
docs.text: This is Debrief v4 running in your browser: the same map, tool forms and results panel as the VS Code extension, and the same Python catalogue, history, tools and importers. Nothing is installed, and nothing you do or import leaves your browser.

docs.title: Things to try
docs.text:
• Select and run a tool. Click BLUE ONE in the outline, then Ctrl-click RED ONE. Closest approach is now on offer. Run it: the line appears on the map, the result opens beside it, and current time moves to the moment it found.
  • Look at a moment. Drag Current time at the top of the side column. Each track's position at that time is a square in its colour.
  • Narrow the time window. Drag either handle of Time window, or the band between them. The map shows the window as you drag: tracks are drawn in full within it and faintly outside it, and the tug's track, which ends at 10:35, loses its label once the window starts after that. Let go and the window is saved in the plot, but it's not a step in History, and Undo leaves it alone.
  • Play. Press ▶, or Space on any of the sliders. Choose a speed: at 60× a minute of the exercise passes each second. Playing stops at the end of the window.
  • A colleague changes the window. A colleague changes the time window, under Try, changes it as if from another computer: Debrief shows theirs and says so.
  • Add an annotation. Add… under Annotation, below the outline, opens a form for a line, area, circle, ellipse, label, marker or note. Type positions as you would write them (37°00.000'N 075°30.000'W), give a circle a radius and a colour, and press Add. Select it and press Change… to restyle it: each is one step in History. North arrow shows the chart's north arrow.
  • Draw on the map. Choose Area on the map's toolbar, click each corner and double-click the last; the map says ranges, bearings and the area as you go. Name it in the form and press Add. Select it and drag a corner, or Tab to a handle and use the arrow keys: each change is one step in History.
  • Clean a track. Select RED ONE and choose Put GPS glitches into the selected track under Try, then Jumps… under Track, below the outline: the jumps found are ringed on the map and listed, all ticked; untick any and Remove the rest as one step. Smooth… shows the track as smoothing would leave it before you apply it. Fixes… lists every fix: choose one (or right-click it on the map) to colour, label or comment on it.
  • Move one fix. Select RED ONE and zoom in until each fix has a small ring: drag one, and only that fix moves; the map says how far, which way and how fast the track would now have to go to reach it and to go on, and warns when that is as fast as a jump. Letting go is one step. Or Tab to a ring and use the arrow keys, or choose Move… in Fixes… and type where it goes. OTG/DR… plots the track by dead reckoning, from its first fix by its recorded courses and speeds, or over the ground again.
  • Import a REP file. Under Import your own, choose a REP file: Debrief asks, for each track, whether it is plotted over the ground (OTG) or by dead reckoning (DR). Tick Use this choice for future track imports to be asked no more; Ask again clears it. A track plotted by dead reckoning is tagged DR in the outline and on the map.
  • Move a track. Select BLUE ONE and drag the filled square: the map says how far and which way, along geodesics. Drag the ring to rotate it about the pivot. Choose Time window on the map to move only the fixes in the window, and watch the joins jump. Drag the diamond beside a track's last fix to shear it: the first fix stays put, and the map gives the new course and speed. Choose Stretch on the map to change only its speed. Move…, Rotate…, Shear…, Stretch…, Split… (at current time) and Merge are under Track, below the outline. Each is one step in History.
  • Read the narrative. The Timeline lists the plot's notes in time order. Choose one and current time moves to it.
  • Undo. Every change is a step in History. Undo replays the plot to the step before. Nothing is deleted: the undone step stays listed, and Redo brings it back.
  • Crash part-way through a save. This stops a save after the new plot file is written but before it replaces the old one, as a power cut would. Reopen the plot: it is exactly as it was before that save, and Debrief says a save was interrupted.
  • Add a plot file. Under Import your own, choose a Debrief plot file (.geojson), such as one a colleague sent you. Its whole history comes with it: undo, redo and going back to a step work on what they did.
  • Work alongside a colleague. A colleague changes the plot shows what happens when someone else saves a change: Debrief shows the latest and tells you. …while your next tool runs, then run a tool: Debrief asks whether to combine the changes or save yours as a new plot. It never overwrites theirs.
  • Import your own file. Choose a REP file or a legacy Debrief .dpf plot. It's read and imported in your browser, and everything that couldn't be imported is listed.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The page plays the part of VS Code. Debrief's webviews run unchanged in frames, and Debrief's Python packages run under Pyodide in a web worker, installed from the same wheels the desktop uses.

The sample exercise is copied into the browser's memory. Every change, undo and crash happens there, and is gone when you close the page.

The first start downloads Pyodide and its packages, about 16 MB, from the jsDelivr CDN (cdn.jsdelivr.net). Later visits use your browser's cache. If your network blocks the CDN, the map still works, and the page says that tools, history and import need Python.

docs.title: Blog
docs.text: Short, frequent posts on what is new in Debrief v4, written in the same pull request as the work they describe.

docs.title: How Debrief v4 fits together
docs.text:
Debrief v4 starts with foundations rather than features. Here is the shape everything else will hang from.

flowchart LR
    subgraph host["VS Code (or the web demo)"]
        ext["Debrief extension<br/>TypeScript"]
        views["Map, outline and tool panels<br/>webviews"]
        ext <--> views
    end

    subgraph python["Per-user Python services"]
        tools["Tool service<br/>MCP over REST"]
        kernel["Kernel<br/>time, units, geodesy, formatting"]
        tools --> kernel
    end

    subgraph disk["Your filesystem"]
        cat["STAC catalogue"]
        plot["Plots: GeoJSON<br/>with provenance inside"]
        src["Imported sources<br/>never modified"]
        cat --> plot
        cat --> src
    end

    schema["One schema in LinkML<br/>generates Python and TypeScript types"]

    ext -- "loopback only,<br/>per-session token" --> tools
    agent["AI agents"] -- MCP --> tools
    tools <--> cat
    ext <--> cat
    schema -.-> ext
    schema -.-> tools

A few choices shape everything:

  • Plots are plain files. A plot is a GeoJSON FeatureCollection, catalogued with STAC and carrying its own provenance. Anyone can read it without Debrief, and access control is simply the folder's permissions.
  • Analysis lives in Python. Every operation is a Python tool served over MCP, so the same tool serves the Debrief interface, an analyst's script and an AI agent. A scientist adds a tool by writing a Python file, without rebuilding Debrief.
  • One vocabulary. Every type that crosses between Python and TypeScript is generated from a single LinkML schema, so the two sides cannot drift apart.
  • Everything is recorded. Each change to a plot is recorded so it can be replayed, which is also how undo works.
  • The web demo runs the same tools. In the browser, the Python tools run under Pyodide; nothing is sent to a server.

The first foundations are in place: the schema and its generated types, and a kernel for time, units, geodesic measurement and display formatting. Three early checks came back positive. The schema approach works end to end; the Python code runs unchanged in the browser; and asking the Python service for each Tote update takes a few milliseconds, well inside the 100 ms an analyst needs to drag the time slider smoothly.

docs.title: Fast enough to drag
docs.text:
When you drag the time slider or a target solution, the numbers must keep up with your hand. We measured whether they will.

The Tote shows range and bearing to other platforms at the current time, and it must update within a tenth of a second of the slider moving. In Debrief v4 those numbers come from the Python service, one request per movement.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Analyst
    participant V as Debrief window
    participant P as Python service
    A->>V: drags time slider
    V->>P: Tote values at new time?
    P-->>V: ranges and bearings (about 2 ms)
    V-->>A: Tote updated
    Note over V,P: next request only once the last returns,<br/>always for the latest time

Each request took about 2 milliseconds, and never more than 7, even with twenty platforms: comfortably inside the tenth of a second.

Dragging a target motion analysis solution is harder, because every bearing in the period must be recomputed. With thousands of bearings, the straightforward code took a fifth of a second, too slow. Computing them all at once instead brought six hours of bearings at one a second down to under 40 milliseconds.

We measured on a development machine, so we will check again on an analyst's laptop before the target motion analysis work begins.

docs.title: Measuring on the real Earth
docs.text:
Debrief v4 measures ranges and bearings along the true shape of the Earth. Legacy Debrief did not, so some figures will change slightly.

Legacy Debrief treated each small patch of sea as flat, with one degree of arc equal to 60 nautical miles. Debrief v4 measures along geodesics on the WGS84 ellipsoid, the same model as GPS, whatever projection the map uses.

In legacy's code, range and bearing (WorldLocation.rangeFrom, bearingFrom and subtract) go through its FlatEarth model. That is mid-latitude sailing: the change in longitude is scaled by the cosine of the mean latitude, and the range in degrees is turned into nautical miles at 60 to the degree (Conversions.Degs2Nm). The desktop application did install a GeoTools calculator, GeoCalculatorAdapter, which is ellipsoidal, but only its bearingBetween method uses it. Everything else, including every range, still used the flat calculation it inherits.

The difference is small but not zero. Worst cases, across every bearing:

Latitude Range Range differs by Bearing differs by 50° 1 nmi 7 m 0.09° 50° 10 nmi 70 m 0.16° 50° 50 nmi 350 m 0.5° 70° 50 nmi 430 m 1.1° 
flowchart LR
    old["Legacy: flat patches<br/>1° = 60 nmi"] -- "about 0.4% apart<br/>at UK latitudes" --> new["v4: WGS84 geodesics"]

Try it: drag A and B and watch the two answers part company. Move them further north, or further apart, and the difference grows. The dashed line is just a straight line on the Mercator chart, which is how neither of them measures.

If you compare a v4 figure with one from an old report, expect differences of this size. Bearing residuals in target motion analysis are the most sensitive: a solution built in legacy Debrief will not show exactly the same residuals in v4.

Every value shown on screen also goes through one formatting service, so knots, nautical miles, three-figure bearings such as 045.0°T, and Zulu times look the same everywhere.

docs.title: Load and look: the whole path, end to end
docs.text:
Phase 1's job is to prove the architecture by walking one path all the way through. You open a catalogue, see a plot on a map, select tracks, run a Python tool, and see its result on the map. That now works in VS Code.

Update, 11 October 2026

The demo below is today's Debrief, so it includes features added since this post was written, such as the time control at the top of the side column and undo.

Every picture here comes from CI. A test drives the real VS Code, with the real extension and the real Python tool service, on Debrief's sample exercise. It takes these screenshots as it goes, so they can't drift from what the software does.

docs.title: Catalogues, plots and the map
docs.text:
The Catalogues view lists the folders Debrief knows about and the plots in each. Here that's the sample exercise: three serials on 15 June 2023, built by the sample data workstream.

Opening a serial shows it on the map:

  • BLUE ONE and RED ONE. These are synthesised exercise tracks. Each was imported from a REP file that is kept, unchanged, as a source.
  • The background picture. The grey tracks are real, anonymised open AIS data.
  • The exercise area. An annotation drawn in amber.

The map is Web Mercator, but every line follows the geodesic: the path a vessel actually takes. A straight line on a Mercator chart is not that path (why it matters).

The Outline shows the plot's features, its supporting files and its reference data. The Tools view shows which tools apply to what is selected.

docs.title: Selecting, and the tools on offer
docs.text:
Select a track on the map or in the outline, and every view follows. The tools view asks the Python tool service which tools apply to everything selected.

  • On offer. With one track selected you're offered Track summary, Range rings and Add note.
  • Not on offer. Closest approach, which needs two tracks, waits under Other tools in VS Code, saying so; in the demo below it is greyed out, with the reason beside it. Nothing is hidden without a reason.

Try it here. Select BLUE ONE in the outline, Ctrl-click RED ONE, and see what's on offer:

docs.title: A form from a declaration
docs.text:
Nobody wrote this form. Debrief builds it from the tool's declaration in Python:

  • the explanation;
  • what the tool will act on;
  • a distance with a unit picker;
  • a whole number;
  • an optional time.

The same declaration tells an AI agent what the tool needs, because the tool service speaks MCP.

docs.title: Running tools
docs.text:
Range rings draws geodesic circles around BLUE ONE at 09:30Z. Closest approach finds when BLUE ONE and RED ONE were nearest: 2.29 nmi at 09:21:17Z, bearing 280.5° from BLUE ONE. It draws the line between them, and puts the figures in a results panel beside the map. The panel repeats the tool's caveat, and says what was saved to the plot and what was not.

Every run that changes the plot is saved with its history: the tool, its version, who ran it, what was selected, and every value on the form. That's the start of being able to replay an analysis from its sources.

Track summary gives the start, end, duration, distance run and mean speed of each selected track. Its explanation warns that a gap in the track shortens the distance.

docs.title: Your theme, our colours
docs.text: Debrief takes its interface colours from your VS Code theme, light, dark or high contrast. The data keeps its own colours whatever the theme: red is red and blue is blue, as in legacy Debrief. A check in CI fails if anyone hard-codes an interface colour.

docs.title: What's underneath
docs.text:
• Configuration. One per-user file lists the catalogues you know. The Python services and the extension read it by the same rules.
  • The tool service. Each user runs their own, listening only on their own machine and requiring a token issued at start-up. Tools run in a separate worker process, so a tool that hangs or crashes fails its own run and nothing else.
  • Four tools. The first four are ordinary Python. CI runs them in the browser under Pyodide too, ready for the web demo.
  • Reviewed before merging. Each piece was reviewed before merging by a panel of specialists:
  • security and protocol;
  • Windows deployment;
  • a scientist writing their first tool;
  • an exercise analyst on the sample data;
  • a VS Code engineer and a human-factors specialist on the interface.

docs.title: Not yet
docs.text:
• No time controller. There is no current time to follow yet (Phase 3).
  • Bearings aren't drawn. They are imported but not shown on the map (Phase 4).
  • No undo. That arrives with replay in Phase 2.
  • Coarse coastline. Proper reference charts come with the reference tile service.

docs.title: Nothing lost: undo, crashes, and a plot shared with others
docs.text:
Phase 2 is about trust. An analyst should be able to try something, take it back, have Debrief die mid-save, or share a plot with a colleague who changes it at the same time, and never lose work or have it overwritten without being told.

As before, every picture comes from the integration test, which drives the real VS Code with the real Python tool service on the sample exercise.

docs.title: Every change is a step
docs.text:
Each change to a plot is now recorded as a step: an import, a tool run, an edit. A step holds two things:

  • What made it: the tool, its version, who ran it, what they selected and every value they gave.
  • What it did: the features added, changed and deleted.

The plot file itself is just the result of applying the steps in order. Debrief can always rebuild it from them, and does so whenever the file and the steps disagree.

The History view lists the steps, newest first.

docs.title: Undo is replay
docs.text:
Undo (Ctrl+Z on the map, the outline or the History view) returns the plot to the step before. Debrief does this by replaying the steps up to that point, never by asking a tool to reverse itself. That's why every tool, including one written by a scientist last week, gets undo for free.

  • Nothing is deleted. The undone step stays in the list, marked undone, and Redo brings it back.
  • Undo leaves view state alone. Current time and the selection stay where they are.
  • A new change after undoing replaces the undone steps. They stay on record, marked replaced, but can't be redone. This was the analysts' choice: a record that never loses anything beats a branching history that's hard to follow.

docs.title: Killed mid-save, and recovered
docs.text:
The test kills a Debrief process part-way through saving a change: after it has written the step, before it has recorded the step as current. When the analyst opens the plot again, Debrief finishes the change and says so: Finished saving a change that was interrupted (step 4).

This works because of the order things are written in:

  1. the step, created so that two writers can never claim the same number;
  2. then where the history stands;
  3. then the plot file.

A crash at any point loses at most the change in progress, and here not even that.

Update, 13 Oct 2026

The steps no longer sit in a folder beside the plot: the plot file now carries its whole history, so the one file an analyst sends a colleague brings undo, redo and every record with it. Each save writes a complete new plot file and only then puts it in place of the old one, so a crash leaves the plot exactly as it was before the save in progress; reopening says a save was interrupted. The history is also checked for changes made outside Debrief. See One file, history included.

docs.title: Someone else changed it
docs.text:
Plots are never locked. Two analysts can open the same plot on a shared folder, and the tool service and an agent can work on it too. Instead of locking, every change says which version of the plot it was made against.

  • While a plot is open. If someone else changes it, Debrief shows the latest and says so.
  • When a tool run meets a change made meanwhile. Debrief asks what to do:
  • if the two changes touch different features, it offers to combine the changes;
  • otherwise it offers to save mine as a new plot, which gets the history the analyst was working from, then their change.

Overlapping changes are never combined automatically.

To try this, use A colleague changes it while your next tool runs in the demo above, then run Closest approach.

docs.title: Current time, shared
docs.text:
Current time, the selection and the viewport are now shared state:

  • The map has a time control along its bottom edge, and marks where each track was at that moment.
  • Other extensions can read and set the state.
  • Tools see it and can change it.

Update, 12 Oct 2026

The time control has moved off the map, to the top of the Debrief sidebar, and now sets the plot's time window and plays too. See One window, one file: the time controller.

Closest approach now moves current time to the moment it found:

docs.title: Colour is not history
docs.text:
Changing a track's colour or hiding a feature on the map is presentation. It travels with the plot, but it isn't a change to the analysis, so it's never recorded in the plot's history or provenance. It's undoable all the same: presentation changes are listed at the top of the History view, and one Ctrl+Z takes back whatever the analyst did last.

Update, 12 Oct 2026

We've changed our minds on this. Analysts told us that turning a blue friendly track red, once it proves hostile, is part of the analysis, and that they want one plot file to hand to a colleague, with nothing beside it. So colour and hiding are now ordinary changes to the plot: recorded in its history with who made them, named there ("Colour of BLUE ONE set to red"), and undone by Ctrl+Z like anything else. View state that should travel with the plot, starting with its time window, is kept inside the plot file, in an island the history ignores: it is never a step and never undone.

docs.title: Also in Phase 2
docs.text:
• Legacy plots. Debrief v3 .dpf files import, with every element that has no v4 equivalent named at the end of the import and recorded in the plot's provenance. Across the 46 legacy sample files, 45 import; the 46th is broken on purpose. Try it with a legacy plot of your own. The file is read in your browser and never uploaded:
  • Logs you can share. Logs record errors and tool runs, but never plot data. Feature names and file paths become short hashes, and tool parameters are logged by name and type, never by value.
  • A newer Debrief, an older catalogue. If saving would write a newer data format into a catalogue colleagues share, Debrief asks first.

Every part of this went through review by an expert panel: data integrity, crash safety and concurrency, a VS Code engineer, and an analyst. Each panel found real problems, including a race that could lock a plot against all further changes and a quick double undo that was reported as a conflict. All of them are fixed, and each has a test that fails without the fix.

docs.title: One schema, two languages
docs.text:
Debrief's analysis runs in Python and its interface in TypeScript. Every piece of data that passes between them is defined once, so the two sides cannot quietly disagree.

flowchart LR
    linkml["LinkML schema<br/>the one definition"]
    json["JSON Schema"]
    py["Python models"]
    ts["TypeScript types"]
    fixtures["Shared test files<br/>valid and broken examples"]

    linkml --> py
    linkml --> json
    json --> ts
    fixtures -. checked by .-> py
    fixtures -. checked by .-> ts

The schema describes plots, catalogues, the history of every change, tools and their parameters, and the analyst's display settings. From it we generate Python and TypeScript code; nobody writes those types by hand.

A few things we settled along the way:

  • Units travel with the numbers. A speed is stored as {"unit": "m/s", "values": [...]}, so a file can never leave you guessing. A speed labelled in degrees is rejected in both languages.
  • A plot is still plain GeoJSON. Positions stay as longitude and latitude in degrees, so any GIS tool can read a plot without Debrief.
  • The same examples test both sides. Over seventy example files, some valid and some deliberately broken, are checked by Python and by TypeScript. A plot written by one and read by the other comes back unchanged.

LinkML needed some help: its TypeScript output was unusable, and a few of its Python and JSON Schema outputs disagreed with each other. Each workaround now has an example file that would catch it coming back.

docs.title: Debrief's Python, in your browser
docs.text:
The public demonstration of Debrief will run its Python analysis tools inside your web browser. We checked that it works before building on it.

Pyodide is Python compiled to run in a browser. We ran the same test under ordinary Python and under Pyodide and compared every answer: geodesic measurements, closest approach, formatted values and over eighty example files.

flowchart LR
    test["Same test script"] --> cp["Ordinary Python"]
    test --> pyo["Python in the browser<br/>(Pyodide)"]
    cp --> cmp{"Identical?"}
    pyo --> cmp
    cmp -- yes --> ok["Pass"]

The answers were identical. Calculations run about half as fast in the browser, and the demonstration needs a few seconds to start.

Half as fast is quick, but not always instant. In the demo below, Closest approach between two four-hour tracks of 241 fixes each takes about 1.5 seconds of Python in Chrome, against 0.8 seconds under ordinary Python on the same machine. From pressing Run to seeing the result takes about 2.5 seconds, because the plot is saved, with its history, and shown again. Building the demo halved that tool's time on every platform: it now works out the geodesic between each pair of fixes once, rather than at every step of its search.

This check now runs on every change. It also sets a rule for the future: any library a Debrief tool relies on must be able to run in the browser too, or the tool must say plainly that it is only available on the desktop.

Nothing in the demonstration leaves your browser, and it only ever holds unclassified sample data.

docs.text: You no longer need to install anything to try Debrief v4. The blog now has demos you can play with: the real map, tool forms and Python tools, running in your browser.

docs.title: It's the real thing
docs.text:
The demos are not mock-ups. They use exactly what the VS Code extension uses:

  • The map, tool form and results panel are Debrief's own webviews, unchanged. The page around them plays the part of VS Code.
  • The Python is Debrief's own: the catalogue, plot history, tools and importers. It runs under Pyodide, installed from the same packages the desktop uses.

The sample exercise is copied into your browser's memory. Every change, undo and crash happens there, and is gone when you close the page. Nothing is sent anywhere.

docs.title: Where to play
docs.text:
• Try Debrief: everything in one place.
  • Load and look: select tracks and see which tools are offered.
  • Nothing lost: undo, a crash mid-save, and a colleague changing the plot while your tool runs. It also has a demo for importing your own legacy .dpf or REP file, which never leaves your browser.
  • Measuring on the real Earth: drag two positions and compare Debrief v4's range and bearing with legacy Debrief's.

docs.title: It already found a bug
docs.text:
Building the demos showed that Pyodide's Python has no hard links, so saving a change failed in the browser. Saving now works there. The Pyodide check that CI runs on every change now saves, changes, undoes and redoes a plot, and requires the same answers as on the desktop.

Every demo is also played in CI, in Chromium, as a reader would play it. If a change breaks a demo, the build fails.

docs.title: One window, one file: the time controller
docs.text:
Debrief now has a time controller. The analyst sets one time window for the whole plot, plays through it at a chosen speed, and hands the plot file to a colleague, who opens it on the same window.

The VS Code picture comes from the integration test, which drives the real VS Code with the real Python tool service on the sample exercise. The others come from the playground test, which plays the demo below in a browser.

docs.title: The controller
docs.text:
In VS Code the controller is the Time view, at the top of the Debrief sidebar. The catalogues, outline, tools and history stay below it. The map no longer has a control along its bottom edge; it only draws. The playground has the same component at the top of its side column. It is compact, so all of it shows at the height VS Code first gives the view, without scrolling: play, the steps and the speed share a line with current time, and the note about a tool's window (below) is one line.

It has three parts:

  • Time window. A slider with two handles over the plot's whole period. Drag a handle to move that end, or the band between them to move the whole window.
  • Current time. A slider over the window, never outside it. ‹ and › step back and forward. The step is about a hundredth of the window, and the controller shows it.
  • Play. ▶ (or Space on any slider) plays current time forward and stops at the end of the window.

The speeds are 1×, 10×, 60×, 600× and 3600× real time. Exercise serials last hours and deployments last weeks, so the speeds run from watching a close-quarters encounter as it happened (1×) to crossing a week in under three minutes (3600×). The default, 60×, plays a minute of the exercise each second, so a four-hour serial takes four minutes.

Everything works from the keyboard. The arrow keys move a handle or current time by a step, Page Up and Page Down by ten, and Home and End to the ends. Each slider says its time to screen readers. The time controller interaction model has the full table.

docs.title: What the map shows
docs.text:
Within the window, tracks are drawn in full: solid lines, direction ticks, a hollow dot at the first fix in the window and a labelled dot at the last. Outside the window, each whole track stays as a thin, solid line in a quieter version of its colour: a context track.

Hiding everything outside the window would be cleaner, but it would lose the shape of the exercise, and for deployments the requirement is to see a whole deployment's tracks at once, with sensor data limited to the window. So the context track stays, with no ticks, dots or labels to compete with the window. It is drawn at least 3:1 against the map on any theme, so it is quiet without being hard to see. A busy plot can draw it faint instead, or make it hidden, from the Time view's ... menu in VS Code (in the playground, the Context list beside the window's length).

Annotations with a time or a period are drawn only while it falls in the window. Annotations without one, such as the exercise area, always are.

Bearings aren't drawn yet. When they are, they'll be drawn only within the window. Weeks of bearings at once would be unreadable, and the window is also how Debrief will keep millions of observations off the screen.

docs.title: Moving shows; letting go saves
docs.text:
The map follows the window as you drag it, but the window is saved only when you let go: when you release the pointer, or the key. Holding an arrow key down saves once.

Saving on every movement would rewrite the plot file many times a second. On a shared folder, a colleague's Debrief would see a stream of changes to the file and have to check each one.

docs.title: One plot file
docs.text:
Analysts asked for one thing above all: a plot they can hand to a colleague as one file, with nothing beside it. That decided where everything lives.

Where it's kept Undo In the history Tracks, annotations, tool results The plot file, through its history Yes Yes A track's colour, what's hidden The plot file, through its history Yes Yes Time window, how context tracks are drawn The plot file, in its island No No Current time, selection, viewport Nowhere: they're shared while the plot is open No No

Colour and hiding are part of the analysis: turning a friendly blue track red once it proves hostile is a judgement, and it belongs in the record. The window isn't. Moving it is how the analyst looks at the plot, not a change to it, and it would swamp the history with steps nobody wants to undo.

So the window lives in the plot's island: a small part of the plot file that the history ignores. The window travels with the file, but:

  • It's never a step. The History view doesn't list it, and its provenance doesn't record it.
  • Undo leaves it alone. Ctrl+Z takes back the last change to the plot, never a move of the window.
  • It never conflicts with a change to the plot. A colleague can run a tool while you move the window, and neither of you is asked anything.

docs.title: A colleague's window
docs.text:
The window is still shared through the file, so two people can change it at once. Debrief watches the plot file as well as its history. When a colleague's window arrives, Debrief shows it without reading the plot's content again, and says so.

If you let go of a window after a colleague changed theirs, yours isn't saved over it. Debrief shows theirs and says: Someone else changed the time window, so yours was not saved. Set it again if you still want yours. That's the same rule as every other change: nothing is silently overwritten.

docs.title: Update, later on 12 Oct: three changes from an expert panel
docs.text:
We asked a panel (an analyst, an interaction designer, an accessibility specialist and a data-integrity reviewer) three questions the first version left open. They agreed unanimously, and the controller now does this:

  • Context tracks you can see. The faint line was too faint on some themes. A context track is now visible by default: at least 3:1 against the map, worked out from the theme for every colour Debrief gives a track. A plot can still draw them faint, or keep them hidden; that choice is saved with the plot, like the window. If you need the contrast everywhere, the setting Debrief › Map: Minimum Context Contrast draws faint as visible on every plot you open. High-contrast themes draw them in full colour.
  • A window of at least a second. The handles stop a second apart and never cross. When the window is too short to play at the chosen speed, Play is off and says why: Window too short to play at 60×: widen it or slow down.
  • A tool's time outside your window is shown, never saved. Closest approach moves current time to the moment it finds. If that's outside your window, the window on screen widens just enough to take it in (to at most twice its length; beyond that it moves instead). The part that differs is hatched, the tool's message adds (outside your saved window), and a note stays until you choose: Keep saves the window shown; Revert goes back to yours. Dragging the window counts as Keep. Nothing a tool does is ever saved as your window behind your back, so a colleague opening the plot sees the window you chose.

  • The window following current time while playing, so a fixed-length window slides along an exercise.
  • Choosing the step. For now it's a hundredth of the window.

docs.title: Annotations
docs.text:
Analysts can now add lines, areas, circles, ellipses, labels, markers and notes to a plot through a form, style them, give them a time, change and delete them. Each is one step in the plot's history, so Ctrl+Z takes it back. Notes are listed in a new Timeline, and legacy plots bring their circles, ellipses and styling with them.

The VS Code pictures come from the integration test, which drives the real VS Code with the real Python tool service on the sample exercise. The others come from the playground test, which plays the demo below in a browser.

docs.title: Forms first
docs.text:
The product owner asked for annotations through forms first, and drawing on the map second. A form is exact: an exclusion zone is "4 km around 37°00.000'N 075°30.000'W", not wherever the pointer landed, and a form works the same from the keyboard, for a screen reader and for an agent.

Add annotation… opens the form beside the map. Choose a kind:

Kind Is Line a line through two or more positions Area a closed area with three or more corners Circle every position at one range from a centre Ellipse an ellipse about a centre, its longer axis along a true bearing Label text at a position Marker a marked position Note text at a time, with no position

Positions are typed the way analysts write them: 50°20.120'N 004°07.210'W, 50 20.12 N 4 7.21 W, N50 20.12 W4 7.21, degrees, minutes and seconds, or two decimals. Under each, the form says what it understood, Means 50°20.120'N 004°07.210'W, so a slip shows before it is saved. Python and TypeScript read positions the same way, held to one shared set of test cases.

A radius, or an ellipse's semi-axes, is a number and a unit (nautical miles, yards, metres or kilometres), and the unit is kept with the value: a circle of 2 nmi stays 2 nmi for an analyst who reads ranges in yards. An ellipse's orientation is degrees true.

Anything wrong is said beside its field (Give the radius, a number more than zero), and nothing is saved until it is right.

docs.title: One step each
docs.text:
Adding an annotation is one step in the plot's history, named so the History view reads like a log: Circle 'Exclusion zone' added. So is every change through the form: Style of Circle 'Exclusion zone' changed when only its look changed, Time of … when only its time did, … renamed …, or Circle 'Exclusion zone' changed for anything else. Deleting is a step too, and named sets keep their other members.

Style is content, the same decision as a track's colour on 12 October: turning a zone red is an analyst's judgement, so it is recorded and undoable. An annotation can have its own colour, a solid, dashed or dotted line of any width, a fill and how opaque it is, and its label's size and place. Left alone, annotations are drawn as before: amber and dashed, so nothing a tool draws is mistaken for a track.

The form is the same path an agent takes. The tool service has debrief/add_annotation, debrief/edit_annotation, debrief/delete_annotations and debrief/set_north_arrow; the forms call them, the playground calls the same Python, and an agent can restyle a zone by sending only {"appearance": {"line_style": "solid"}}.

docs.title: Circles in a format without curves
docs.text:
GeoJSON, which plot files are, has no circles. We had two choices:

  • A point with a radius. Small and exact, but any other GeoJSON tool would show a point, and a plot's extent (what "zoom to plot" fits) would leave the circle out.
  • A polygon approximating it, with the exact centre and size beside it. Other tools see the area; Debrief reads the centre and size.

We chose the second. A circle or an ellipse is a polygon of 72 sides, each corner reached along the geodesic from the centre, so QGIS or geojson.io draws the zone. Its shape, centre, radius (or semi_major, semi_minor and orientation), each with its unit, are ordinary properties. Debrief draws it from those, smoothly and along geodesics at any zoom, and the form edits those. Change the radius and the polygon is made again; a rule checked on reading refuses a polygon that no longer matches its centre and size, so the two can't drift apart.

docs.title: Time, and the Timeline
docs.text:
An annotation can have a time, a period, or none. With a time or a period it is drawn only while that falls in the time window, as the time controller already does for annotations tools draw; with none, always.

Notes have a time and no position, so they don't appear on the map. They are in the new Timeline: a view under the outline listing the plot's notes and periods in time order. The sample exercise's narrative (Bow sonar contact, Contact classified submarine) is there already. Choose an entry and current time moves to it; the map and every other view follow. The entry current time is at is marked, and in VS Code the view keeps it in sight while playing, so the narrative can be read along with the replay.

If the entry's time is outside the window you're looking at, the window widens or moves to show it, without saving anything: the same rule as for a tool's time, with Keep and Revert on the time controller.

It is deliberately simple: a list, not a chart. It's a native view in VS Code, so it works from the keyboard and with screen readers like every other view.

docs.title: Chart furniture
docs.text: The scale bar was already there, in the analyst's distance unit. A plot can now carry a north arrow: North arrow on the Outline view's menu adds it, and removes it again, as a step. The map is Web Mercator, so north is up everywhere and the arrow simply points up. Grids, legends and inset maps aren't done; they wait for a need.

docs.title: Legacy plots keep their look
docs.text:
The .dpf importer listed colours, fonts, fills and line styles of annotations as not imported, and turned circles and ellipses into anonymous polygons. Now a legacy circle is a circle, with its centre and radius, and an ellipse keeps its axes and orientation. Each annotation keeps its colour, its line style and width, its fill (semi-transparent or solid), its label's size and its label's place. Those leave the list of what wasn't imported.

Some of the legacy look has no v4 equivalent yet, so it is still listed, counted and named: label symbols (Carrier, Wreck), fonts other than plain Arial (the size is kept), label colours that differ from the line, arrowheads, and the dash patterns v4 doesn't have (long dashes, short dashes and dot-dash are drawn dashed; unconnected points dotted). The .dpf file stays in the catalogue as the plot's source, so re-importing it later recovers what a later version can hold.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text: Press Add annotation… under the outline, name a circle, give it a radius and a colour, and press Add. Select it, press Change…, make it solid and filled, and save. Then Ctrl+Z: the style goes back. Choose an entry in the Timeline and watch current time move:

docs.title: Not yet
docs.text:
• Drawing on the map. Placing and dragging positions with the pointer is part B.

Update, 13 Oct 2026

Annotations can now be drawn on the map, and changed there with handles or the arrow keys. See Drawing on the map.

  • Arrowheads, label symbols and more chart furniture. Listed when a legacy plot has them.
  • Changing an annotation's kind once made: delete it and add another.
  • Circles across the antimeridian are drawn whole in Debrief, but their polygon, for other tools, is not split there as GeoJSON advises.

docs.title: Drawing on the map
docs.text:
Annotations can now be drawn straight onto the map: a line, an area, a circle, an ellipse, a label or a marker, with the range, bearing and size shown as you draw. Select one and handles appear, to drag a corner, move a circle or turn an ellipse. Each finished annotation is one step in the plot's history, and so is each change, so Ctrl+Z takes it back. Everything can also be done from the keyboard.

The playground pictures come from the playground test, which plays the demo below in a browser with the pointer and the keyboard. The VS Code picture comes from the integration test, which drives the real VS Code with the real Python tool service.

docs.title: A toolbar on the map
docs.text:
This morning's post added annotations through a form, which is exact: "4 km around 37°00.000'N 075°30.000'W". Often, though, an analyst wants a box around where the contacts were, or a circle about there. That's quicker to draw than to type.

The map now has a small toolbar under the zoom buttons: Line, Area, Circle, Ellipse, Label, Marker and Cancel. Choose one and the map changes mode: the button stays pressed, the map gets a focus outline, the pointer becomes a cross, and a note at the top says what to do next. It doesn't touch current time, the time window or the selection.

For a line or an area, click each position or corner, and double-click the last (or press Enter). Backspace takes away the last point; Escape stops and keeps nothing. As you go, the map says what you've drawn in your own units: the leg to the pointer, the range and bearing back to the start, and the length so far or the area enclosed. Ranges and bearings are along geodesics, like everything else Debrief measures (see Measuring on the real Earth).

docs.title: Circles and ellipses
docs.text:
A circle is a centre and a radius: click the centre and click again at the radius, or press at the centre and drag outwards. The note says the radius, its bearing and the area inside it as you drag.

The radius that's saved is the one the note showed, in your length unit and to the decimals you read lengths to. If the note said 4.31 nmi, the plot holds 4.31 nmi, not 4.30862.

An ellipse takes three clicks: the centre, the end of the longer axis (which sets its orientation) and a point to one side, which sets the width. The side can't make the shorter axis the longer: the width stops at the length of the longer axis, where the ellipse is a circle.

Labels and markers are one click.

docs.title: Naming it is the step
docs.text:
When you finish drawing, the annotation form opens beside the map, with the kind, corners and size already filled in and the cursor in Name. Name it, give it a time or a style if you like, and press Add. That's one step in the History view: Area 'Patrol box' added. Cancel keeps nothing, and the dashed sketch leaves the map.

We considered adding the annotation as soon as it's drawn, with a made-up name like "Area 1", and opening the form afterwards. That makes two steps for one annotation, added then renamed, so Ctrl+Z would undo only the name, and made-up names would end up in plots. Opening the form first means one step per annotation, named by you, and nothing in the history if you change your mind.

docs.title: Handles
docs.text:
Select an annotation on its own and handles appear in the theme's focus colour:

  • Line or area: a square at each corner, a small dashed circle between each pair, and a filled circle in the middle that moves the whole thing.
  • Circle: its centre, which moves it, and its radius.
  • Ellipse: its centre, the end of its longer axis (length and orientation) and its side (width).
  • Label or marker: its position.

Drag a handle and the annotation follows, with the note saying what it now measures. Let go and the change is saved as one step, named for what you did: Circle 'Keep clear' moved, Circle 'Keep clear' resized, Area 'Patrol box' reshaped. Drag a dashed handle between two corners to add a corner there. Press Escape before letting go and it goes back, with nothing recorded.

If a colleague (or an agent) changes the plot while you're dragging, Debrief shows their change at once, drops your drag and says so. Your change isn't made on top of theirs; drag again if it still applies. That is the same rule as for tools and undo: nothing is ever silently overwritten.

docs.title: Without a mouse
docs.text:
The forms already let you type every position and size exactly. Drawing and handles work from the keyboard too:

  • Drawing: Tab to the toolbar and press Enter on a kind. A cross appears in the middle of the map; the arrow keys pan the map under it, Space places a point at the cross, and Enter finishes.
  • Handles: Tab to one. Each is named for screen readers, such as Area 'Patrol box': corner 2 of 4; drag it, or use the arrow keys; Delete removes it. The arrow keys move it 5 pixels at a time, or 25 with Shift. A run of presses is saved as one step when you stop, rather than one step per press, which would bury the History view. Escape puts it back first. Delete removes a corner, unless that would leave an area with fewer than three.

docs.title: In VS Code
docs.text: It's the same map in VS Code: the same toolbar, the same handles, the same form beside the map, and the same steps through the Python tool service.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text: Choose Area on the map's toolbar, click three or four corners and double-click the last. Name it and press Add. Then drag a corner, and press Ctrl+Z. Or Tab to the toolbar and do it all from the keyboard:

docs.title: Not yet
docs.text:
• Snapping to a track, a fix or another annotation's corner. Use the form when it needs to be exact.
  • Rotating a whole line or area.
  • Moving several annotations at once. Handles appear on an annotation selected on its own.
  • Touch. The handles take pointer events, so a pen or a finger can drag them, but drawing on a tablet hasn't been tried.

docs.title: One file, history included
docs.text:
A plot is now one file an analyst can pass to a colleague, and its whole history goes with it. The colleague can undo a step the sender made, go back to any step, and see who did what, with nothing else beside the file.

The pictures come from the integration test, which drives the real VS Code with the real Python tool service on the sample exercise.

docs.title: What the product owner decided
docs.text:
On 13 October the product owner settled three questions:

  1. A plot is one file. plot.geojson carries the plot's content, its view (the island) and its full history: every step, with what made it and what it changed, its provenance, whether it is undone or replaced, and which step is current. Pass the file and you pass undo, redo, going back to a step, and provenance.
  2. Sources are not transported. When Debrief first imports a REP or .dpf file, the imported tracks and annotations are recorded in the plot's first step. Replay starts from that step, so it never needs the original file. A catalogue may keep its sources for audit, and the history still names each source and its checksum, but the plot file doesn't depend on them.
  3. Keep all history, always. No limit on steps, no folding, no "flatten history" command.

Until now the history lived in a history folder beside the plot: one file per step and a file saying which step was current. That made a plot a folder, not a file.

docs.title: Sending a plot to a colleague
docs.text:
The analyst sends serial 1 as a single file. The colleague uses Add a plot file… on the Catalogues view (the button with the plus on a page) and chooses it. Debrief checks the history, adds the plot to the catalogue and says how many steps came with it.

The History view lists the sender's steps exactly as they were: the import, two tool runs (the second undone, then replaced), a note added by a colleague, the colour change, the hidden track, and Show all. The newest step, Added from a plot file, records the arrival: its note names the file (serial-1-from-ian.geojson) and the catalogue, and it records who added it. No earlier step is changed.

The colleague then presses Ctrl+Z. The step recording the arrival changes nothing on the map, so an undo that took back only that would seem to do nothing. Instead, Ctrl+Z takes it back together with the change before it: the sender's Show all, so the cargo track the sender had hidden is hidden again, and the map says 1 hidden. The History view marks both as next to undo beforehand. Redo brings both back. To go further, Go back to this step on any step works as it did for the sender.

One thing doesn't come across: a step the sender had undone and not redone. It comes with the history, but the step recording the arrival is made after the plot as the sender left it, so the sender's undone step is now replaced by a later change, as it would be if the sender had made a new change. It can be read, but not redone.

If the plot is already in the catalogue (the same file added twice, or a plot sent back with changes), the new one is listed as Serial 1 (from serial-1-from-ian.geojson), so the two can be told apart. The plot's own title is unchanged.

You can try this in the playground: under Import your own, choose a Debrief plot file (.geojson). It's added in your browser and never uploaded.

docs.title: Checked for changes made outside Debrief
docs.text:
A plot file is a text file, and someone might edit it. The product owner asked that the history be protected, not trusted blindly. So:

  • Each step carries a checksum that covers the step and the step before it. Change a step, remove one or swap two, and the chain breaks.
  • The current step records the checksum of the plot's content, so content edited without changing the history is noticed too.
  • The view is outside every checksum. A new time window is never mistaken for an edit.

When something doesn't match, Debrief says so in plain words, and never carries on silently:

  • "This plot's history has been changed outside Debrief: step 2 of its history is not as Debrief recorded it." The plot is shown as its file holds it, but undo, redo and changes are refused. A file like this is refused by Add a plot file… too.
  • "This plot's history does not match its content: it may have been edited outside Debrief." The plot is rebuilt from its history, and the file as found is kept beside it.

The checksums catch mistakes and edits made without Debrief. They are not a signature: someone who sets out to forge a history can work out new checksums. Protecting a plot from a determined forger is a job for the folder's permissions and the network it sits on (SEC-01). What Debrief does make sure of is that a history it can't rebuild is never trusted: Add a plot file… replays the history and refuses a file whose steps don't give the plot it holds, and going back to a step replays to it and refuses if that doesn't give the plot the step recorded, so a forged history can't make Debrief write a broken plot.

docs.title: Crash safety, simpler
docs.text:
Every change now rewrites the whole plot file. Debrief writes the new file in full under a temporary name, makes sure it is on the disk, and only then puts it in place of the old one. So the plot file is always the whole plot before the change or the whole plot after it.

The integration test still kills a Debrief process part-way through a save, now just before the new file replaces the old one. Opening the plot again shows it exactly as it was, and says A save was interrupted before it finished, so the plot is as it was before that change. Nothing else was lost. The machinery that finished half-written changes has gone, because there is no half-written change any more.

Plots that still have a history folder have it moved into their plot file the first time someone who can write opens them. Debrief replays the moved history, checks it gives the same plot, and only then removes the folder. Before the data format reaches 1.0 only plots of the current format open at all, so in practice this rarely runs.

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text:
One file holding everything is bigger, and every change rewrites it. We measured on a synthetic plot of 40 tracks and 100,000 fixes (10.8 MB of content) with 200 steps, before and after:

History in a folder History in the plot file On disk 48.2 MB, in about 200 files 27.6 MB, one file Make a change 6.0 s 4.4 s Undo 2.0 s 0.7 s Redo 2.0 s 0.7 s Read the plot again 0.5 s 0.4 s Open in a new session, with its history listed 14 to 15 s 14 to 16 s

On the sample exercise's serial 1 (0.4 MB) every one of these takes a quarter of a second or less, before and after. Most of the time on the large plot went on checking the plot's content against the data format, every feature of it, for every change.

So now each feature is checked once. A feature's check depends on that feature alone, so one that has passed (in the plot as read, or in the step that added it) isn't checked again; a change checks the features it adds or changes, and the rules that span the whole plot (no two features with one id, every named set naming features the plot has) still run every time. Measured again on the same synthetic plot (18.6 MB with its history, on another machine), before and after:

Every feature, every time Each feature once Make a change 4.5 s 1.0 to 1.5 s Undo or redo 0.6 s 0.7 s Change the time window 1.1 s 0.6 s Open in a new session, with its history listed 9.4 s 7.2 s Add the plot file to another catalogue 14.5 s 8.6 s

Opening in a new session still checks every step once, every feature in it included: a plot file read from disk, or received from someone, is never taken on trust. Undo and redo rebuild the plot by replaying its steps, whose features were all checked when the steps were read, and then check that the plot they give is the one the step recorded.

The history is written one step a line, without the indentation the content has, which keeps the file far smaller than indenting it would. Checks are only done once: steps this process has already checked are not checked again, and when another process adds a step, only that step is.

docs.title: Also
docs.text:
• The STAC item is now just catalogue metadata: title, period and extent, all derived from the plot file. The plot file alone is enough to make it again, which is what Add a plot file… does.
  • Changes made elsewhere are spotted by watching the plot file alone: Debrief compares the history's current step, how many steps it has, and the content checksum the current step recorded. A colleague's new time window changes none of those, so Debrief shows the new window without reading the whole plot again.
  • Save as new after a conflict now copies the history up to the analyst's starting point unchanged, checksums and all.

docs.title: Cleaning tracks: jumps, smoothing and marking fixes
docs.text:
Three ways to tidy a track have arrived. Jump removal finds fixes a platform could not have reached in time, shows them to you on the map and in a list, and removes the ones you confirm. Smoothing shows you the track as it would be, and how far it would move each fix, before you apply it. And single fixes can now have a colour, a label or a comment of their own, as they could in legacy Debrief, so legacy plots no longer lose them on import. Each is one step in the plot's history, and Ctrl+Z takes it back.

The playground pictures come from the playground test, which plays the demo below in a browser. The VS Code pictures come from the integration test, which drives the real VS Code with the real Python tool service. By then, earlier steps of the tests have moved, split and coloured some of the tracks.

docs.title: Nothing removed unseen
docs.text:
Real tracks have glitches: a GPS fix a few miles off, a position typed with one digit wrong. Each looks like the platform leapt somewhere and back. Debrief calls such a fix a jump: a fix the platform could not have reached in time from the last good fix before it.

How fast is too fast? It depends on the platform. A helicopter does 120 knots; a submarine on patrol, 5. So the speed Debrief offers is three times the track's median speed between fixes, and never less than 10 knots. Three times the median is far above any change of speed a real platform makes between fixes; the floor stops a stopped or slow platform's position noise from counting. You can change it: type 30, 30 kn or 15 m/s, and the form says what it understood.

Debrief compares each fix with the last good fix, not just the one before it, so a burst of two or three bad fixes in a row is found whole; and a fix only counts as back on the track when the track carries on from it. A track that goes somewhere and stays (a ship at anchor getting under way, say) isn't a jump, and nor is a real burst of speed the track carries on smoothly from (a sprint between drifts), so nothing is offered.

What it finds, it shows. Each jump is ringed on the map, the note at the top says RED ONE: 3 jumps found, each faster than 30.0 kn to reach, and the list beside the map gives each one's time, position and how fast the platform would have had to go. Every jump starts ticked. Untick any that are real (its ring goes), and Remove takes out the rest as one step: RED ONE: 3 jumps removed.

The step's notes say when the jumps were and the speed they were found at, so a colleague reading the history later can see exactly what went. Every series stays in step: the positions, times, speeds, courses, depths and marked fixes all lose the same fixes.

docs.title: Smoothing, previewed
docs.text:
A track recorded by a noisy sensor wobbles. Smooth… takes each fix to the average position of itself and the fixes either side: 5 fixes unless you say, always an odd number, so each fix sits in the middle of its window. We chose this one method, a moving average, because you can say exactly what it did; a simplifier that drops fixes is a different operation, and isn't offered.

It's worked out properly on the earth. Each fix's neighbours are measured as ranges and bearings from it, along geodesics, averaged, and the fix moved by that average, so it's as right far north or across the date line as in the Channel. Near the ends of what you smooth the window narrows evenly, so the first and last fixes never move, and times never change. A gap in the data counts as an end too: fixes either side of a long stretch with none (more than ten times the usual time between fixes) are never averaged together. Recorded courses and speeds are averaged over the same fixes, courses as directions, so 350° and 010° come out as 000°, not 180°.

Before anything changes, the smoothed track is drawn dashed over the track as it is, and the note says what it would do: RED ONE smoothed over 5 fixes, if applied: 236 fixes moved; the most a fix moved: 0.06 nmi, at 09:22:00Z. Apply makes it one step; Cancel changes nothing.

docs.title: A colour, a label or a comment for one fix
docs.text:
Legacy Debrief let you colour one fix red, label it Turn 1, or note that the navigator doubted it. Our .dpf import has, until now, had to say fix comments not imported. Now a fix can carry any of the three. Right-click a fix on the map (on a touch screen, press and hold it), or open the fix list (every fix of the track, with its time, position, course, speed and any mark) and choose one; then Colour…, Label… or Comment….

On the map, a coloured fix is a dot in its colour, and the line from it to the next fix is drawn in it too, as legacy Debrief drew it. A label sits beside its fix. A comment shows when you point at the fix, and it's in the Timeline, at the fix's time, alongside the narrative. Each change is one step: RED ONE fix at 08:40:00Z labelled 'Turn 1'.

How should a plot file hold them? A track keeps its fixes as parallel lists (positions, times, speeds, courses, depths). We could have added three more, a colour, a label and a comment for every fix; but most fixes have none, and a track of 10,000 fixes would carry 30,000 empty entries. Instead each track has a short list of marked fixes, each found by its fix's time, not its place in the list. That choice does real work: remove three jumps before a marked fix and its mark is still on it; split the track and each part keeps its own marks; merge them and they come back together; move, rotate or smooth it and nothing about the marks changes. And the plot is still plain GeoJSON to any other tool.

Legacy plots bring theirs in. A .dpf file's per-fix colours, labels and comments are imported as marked fixes. Legacy Debrief labels every fix with its time unless told otherwise, so a label that only repeats the fix's time isn't imported (Debrief shows times itself), and the import says how many it skipped. Here is the legacy sample plot's NEL_STYLE track, its fixes in their own colours and labelled as they were saved:

docs.title: In VS Code
docs.text:
The same commands sit on the outline's menu for a track: Find and remove jumps…, Smooth track… and Fixes: colour, label or comment…. The jumps are listed in a VS Code list, all ticked; the fix list is a list you can type a time into.

Agents get the same through the tool service: debrief/find_jumps and debrief/preview_smoothing look without changing anything, and debrief/remove_jumps, debrief/smooth_track and debrief/mark_fix change the plot, one step each, with who asked and what they asked for in the step's record.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text: Select RED ONE, choose Put GPS glitches into the selected track under Try (the playground records that as a step of its own, so it's never mistaken for real data), then Jumps… under Track, below the outline. Then Smooth…, and Fixes…, or right-click a fix on the map (press and hold it on a touch screen):

  • Where a legacy label goes (above, below, left or right of its fix), and fix symbols and arrows, which the import still lists.

docs.title: Moving and splitting tracks
docs.text:
A track can now be moved and rotated on the map: the whole track, or only its fixes in the time window. Drag a handle and the track follows, with the range and bearing (or the angle) shown as you go; let go and it's one step in the plot's history. Tracks can also be split at current time and merged again. Everything can be done from the keyboard or a form, and Ctrl+Z takes any of it back.

The playground pictures come from the playground test, which plays the demo below in a browser with the pointer and the keyboard. The VS Code pictures come from the integration test, which drives the real VS Code with the real Python tool service. By the time they reach BLUE ONE, earlier steps of the tests have coloured it red and added a few annotations.

docs.title: Why move a track at all?
docs.text:
Debrief's data comes from many places: a ship's navigation log, a submarine's own estimate of where it was, a plot reconstructed afterwards. They rarely agree exactly. An analyst who knows that RED ONE was at the datum buoy at 09:30 needs to slide RED ONE's track over so that it was, or turn it a few degrees about a fix they trust. Legacy Debrief has done this for years with its drag track tool, and analysts rely on it.

The product owner's decision, yesterday: as in legacy Debrief, dragging moves the whole track, or a selected time period of it, by translation or by rotation about a pivot. Dragging single fixes comes later.

docs.title: Three handles
docs.text:
Select a track on its own and three handles appear in the theme's focus colour:

  • a filled square on a fix in the middle of the track, to move it;
  • a ring beyond the fix farthest from the pivot, on a dashed arm, to rotate it;
  • the pivot, a dotted ring, which the track turns about. Unless you move it, it's on the fix nearest current time.

Drag the square and the track follows the pointer. The track as it was stays on the map, dashed, so you can see how far you've come, and the note at the top says by how much: BLUE ONE: moving 5.02 nmi 056.4°T. Let go and that's one step in the History view, named as the note said it: BLUE ONE moved 5.02 nmi 056.4°T. Press Escape before letting go and it goes back, with nothing recorded.

Drag the ring round the pivot and the track turns with it: BLUE ONE: rotating 24.5° anticlockwise about 37°07.738'N 075°18.960'W.

docs.title: Along geodesics, not across the chart
docs.text:
Everything Debrief measures is along geodesics on the WGS84 ellipsoid (see Measuring on the real Earth), and moving a track is no different. A move takes every fix the same range along the same true bearing, each along its own geodesic. That is not the same as adding the same change of latitude and longitude to every fix, which is how an annotation's whole-shape move works and how you'd slide a track across a paper chart. Near the equator the two hardly differ; far north they do, because a degree of longitude shrinks as you go towards the pole, so a latitude-and-longitude shift would move some fixes further than others. Moving every fix the same distance doesn't keep a track's shape exactly either: on a curved earth nothing short of turning the whole globe does. Far north, a track moved north comes out a little shorter east-west, as the meridians close in, but for the moves an analyst makes it's small: 0.25% for a track at 60° north moved 5 nmi, which is why the speeds recorded with the fixes are kept rather than worked out again. The tests check a track at 88° north and one crossing the antimeridian: every fix moves exactly the distance asked, along exactly the bearing asked.

A rotation keeps each fix's range from the pivot and turns its bearing from the pivot by the angle. The courses recorded with the fixes turn with them, by the angle near the pivot and by a little more or less far from it, where the meridians converge, so each course still points along the track as drawn; speeds and times don't change.

docs.title: Only part of a track
docs.text:
Sometimes only an hour of a track is wrong: a navigation fault, say, between two fixes you trust. Choose Time window in the small Move or rotate control on the map, and only the fixes in the time window move or turn.

We didn't stretch the rest of the track to meet them. The fixes before and after stay exactly where they were, so the track jumps where the moved part meets them, and the map shows that while you drag, saying only the fixes in the time window move, so the track jumps where they meet the rest. A jump you don't want is for jump removal, which comes next, and which you'll then see doing its job rather than something done quietly on your behalf.

The step says so too: BLUE ONE part moved 4.59 nmi 134.9°T, with Only the fixes from 09:40:00Z to 10:20:00Z as its second note.

docs.title: Exactly, or without a mouse
docs.text:
Move track… on the outline's menu (Move… under the outline in the playground) asks what moves, how far and which way. Type 2 km, 1.2 nmi or just 1.2 in your own unit, and a bearing like 045; the form says what it understood (Means 1.08 nmi) before you commit. Rotate track… asks about which fix (nearest current time, first or last, or in VS Code any position you type) and by how much: 12, 12 clockwise or 12 anticlockwise.

From the keyboard, Tab to a handle. The arrow keys move the square 5 pixels at a time (25 with Shift), and turn the ring 1° (10° with Shift), Right and Up clockwise. A run of presses is saved as one step when you stop, not one step per press; Escape puts it back first.

docs.title: Split and merge
docs.text:
Split track at current time… splits the selected track in two, offering BLUE ONE (1) and BLUE ONE (2) as the names, which you can change. Both keep the track's colour and provenance; the first keeps its identity, so anything that referred to the track still does; sensor observations from the split time on go with the second.

Merge selected tracks joins two or more tracks into one, in time order. Tracks that overlap in time aren't merged: we considered asking which track should win where they overlap, and chose a plain refusal instead, which says exactly where the overlap is: The tracks were not merged: they overlap in time (BLUE ONE and RED ONE from 08:00:00Z to 12:00:00Z). Split or move one first, then merge. Merging asks for the merged track's name, offering the earliest's, or BLUE ONE again for BLUE ONE (1) and BLUE ONE (2). If some of the tracks have courses, speeds or depths and others don't, only what every track has can be kept, so Debrief says which would go and asks before merging.

docs.title: In VS Code
docs.text: Same map, same handles, same steps. The integration test moves BLUE ONE as its handle does, rotates it, moves only part of RED ONE, splits it and merges it again.

docs.title: Every step has its reasons
docs.text: Each operation's step records who made it, which tracks it chose and what was asked: the distance and bearing, the angle and the pivot's position, the period, the time of a split and the names of its parts. An agent doing the same through the tool service (debrief/edit_track, debrief/split_track, debrief/merge_tracks) leaves the same record, so a moved track is as traceable as a tool's output. If a colleague changes the plot while you're dragging, Debrief shows their change, drops your drag and says so; nothing is overwritten.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text: Select BLUE ONE in the outline and drag the filled square. Then drag the ring. Choose Time window on the map, narrow the window in the time controller, and drag again to see the joins jump. Try Split at current time… and Merge under the outline, and Ctrl+Z:

docs.title: Shear and stretch
docs.text:
A track, or its fixes in the time window, can now be sheared: hold one end, drag the other, and every fix in between moves in proportion to its time from the end you held. A straight leg stays a straight leg, with a new course and speed, and the map tells you both as you drag. Stretch does the same with the speed alone. Each release is one step, and the keyboard and two small forms do it too.

The playground pictures come from the playground test, which plays the demo below in a browser with the pointer and the keyboard. The VS Code pictures come from the integration test, which drives the real VS Code with the real Python tool service. By the time they reach RED ONE and BLUE ONE, earlier steps of the tests have moved and turned both.

docs.title: Why shear first
docs.text:
When an analyst works up a target motion analysis (TMA), the solution is a set of legs: straight lines, each run at a steady speed. The bearings pin one end of a leg reasonably well; what's uncertain is where the target went from there. Legacy Debrief's answer was to shear the leg: keep one end where it is and drag the other, so the course and speed change together. The product owner told us yesterday that this is the drag analysts use most with TMA legs, so it comes before the rest of the track tidying (jump removal, smoothing, dragging single fixes).

The live bearing residuals that make this a full TMA tool belong to the TMA module, which comes later. What arrives today is the drag itself, on any track, so it can be tried, tested and argued about now.

docs.title: Two diamonds
docs.text:
Select a track on its own and, beside the move and rotate handles from the last post, two diamonds appear: one beside its first fix and one beside its last. Here RED ONE's leg between 09:40 and 10:20, a straight run at a steady 4 knots, with Time window chosen on the map so only that leg changes:

Drag the diamond at the end. The start stays exactly where it is, the end follows the pointer, and every fix in between moves part of the way: a third of the way for a fix a third of the way through the leg in time, and so on. The note at the top gives the new course and speed, and how far the end has gone: RED ONE: shearing to 258.6°T 4.4 kn; end moved 1.16 nmi 324.8°T.

Let go, and it's one step in the History view, named by what the leg now makes good: RED ONE part sheared: 258.6°T 4.4 kn, with Held at the start, 09:40:00Z and the course and speed it made good before as its notes. Only the fixes in the window changed, so the track jumps where they meet the rest of it, just as a move does.

Choose Stretch under Drag the ends on the map and the diamonds get a double edge. Now only how far you drag along the leg counts: the course stays, and the note gives the new speed against the old, RED ONE: stretching to 5.5 kn (was 4.0 kn).

docs.title: The geometry, on a curved earth
docs.text:
The obvious way to shear on a chart is to slide each fix by a fraction of the end's move: a third of the distance, along the same bearing. On the earth that isn't quite right. Meridians close in towards the poles, so "the same bearing" points in slightly different directions at different fixes, and a sheared leg would come out very slightly bent: tens of metres over a 10 nmi leg at 50° north, more further north.

So Debrief works from the end you're holding. Every fix is placed by its range and true bearing from that end, measured along geodesics as everything in Debrief is (see Measuring on the real Earth). Seen that way, any geodesic through the held end is a straight line, and ranges from it are exact. The shear is done there, so a straight leg at a steady speed comes out exactly straight and steady, at 50° north, at 84° north or across the antimeridian; the tests check all three. A stretch keeps each fix's bearing from the held end and scales its range, so a leg stays on its own line.

The courses and speeds recorded with each fix aren't thrown away and worked out again from the new positions, which would replace what the log recorded with the jitter of the fixes. They're carried through the same change instead: a shear adds the leg's change of velocity to each fix's own, so a fix that the log says was steering 000 at 10 knots, on a leg that has just gained 10 knots east, now says 045 at 14.1 knots. On a clean straight leg, every fix ends up with exactly the leg's new course and speed.

docs.title: Keyboard and forms
docs.text:
Tab to a diamond. Shearing, the arrow keys move it 5 pixels at a time (25 with Shift). Stretching, Up makes the leg 0.1 knots faster and Down 0.1 knots slower (1 knot with Shift). As with every handle, a run of presses is one step, not one per press.

For an exact answer there's Shear track… on the outline's menu (Shear… under Track, below the outline, in the playground): which end stays, then the course and speed you want the leg to make good, offered as what it makes good now. Stretch track… asks only for the speed. Speeds can be typed in knots, metres per second or kilometres an hour.

docs.title: In VS Code
docs.text: The same map, diamonds and steps. The integration test shears BLUE ONE as its end would, then through Shear track… and Stretch track… with values given, as an agent does through debrief/edit_track, and opens the form.

docs.title: Every step has its reasons
docs.text: Each shear or stretch records which end was held and when, how far and which way the other end went, and the course and speed the leg then made good. An agent doing the same through the tool service leaves the same record, and Ctrl+Z takes any of it back.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text: Select RED ONE, narrow the time window to one of its legs, choose Time window on the map, and drag the diamond at the leg's end. Then choose Stretch and drag again, or try Shear… under Track, below the outline:
