docs.title: Dragging a fix, and dead reckoning
docs.text:
The last of the track operations has arrived. Zoom in on a track and each fix has a small ring of its own: drag one, and only that fix moves. Its time stays, its neighbours stay, and the map tells you, as you drag, how fast the platform would now have to go to reach it and to carry on. And the legacy OTG and DR modes are back, the legacy way: import a REP file and Debrief asks, for each track, whether it is plotted over the ground or dead reckoned from its courses and speeds, and you can tell it to use that choice for future imports. Each change to a plot is one step, and Ctrl+Z takes it back.

The playground pictures come from the playground test, which plays the demo below in a browser with the mouse, a finger and the keyboard. The VS Code pictures come from the integration test, which drives the real VS Code with the real Python tool service. By then, earlier steps of the tests have moved, split and cleaned the tracks.

docs.title: One fix, the legacy way
docs.text:
We asked the product owner how a single-fix drag should behave, and the answer was: as legacy Debrief did, unless there's a reason not to. So only the fix you grab moves. Nothing either side of it is stretched or smoothed to meet it, its time is unchanged, and if it carries a colour, a label or a comment of its own, that stays with it (marks are found by their fix's time, as the last post explained).

The one real question was the fix's course and speed. A plot holds, for each fix, the course and speed the platform logged. When you move a fix, should Debrief work them out again from the new positions? We decided not to, for the same reason a move of the whole track keeps them: they are what the platform's compass and log (or its GPS) said, not something Debrief derived from where the fix was plotted, and a fix plotted in the wrong place doesn't change what the ship was doing. Recomputing them would quietly swap logged data for guesses.

What the new position implies is still worth knowing, though, so Debrief says it: the speed needed to reach the fix from the one before, and to get from it to the one after, each along the geodesic. Pull a fix too far and the note says so: faster than 15.0 kn, as a jump would be, using the same threshold jump removal offers.

Let go, and that's one step in the history: RED ONE fix at 09:43:00Z moved 0.31 nmi 056.5°T, with notes giving the new position and the speeds before and after.

docs.title: Rings only when you can grab one
docs.text:
A track of 241 fixes, seen whole, is a line of dots a pixel or two apart; rings on all of them would bury it, and you'd grab the wrong one. So the rings appear only when you've zoomed in far enough that the fixes are apart on the screen (at least 14 pixels, and no more than 60 in view). Until then, the note at the top says Zoom in to move a single fix.

We considered a single ring that follows the pointer to the nearest fix instead. We chose rings that are simply there, once you're close enough, because they work the same with a finger (a tablet has no pointer to hover) and from the keyboard: Tab reaches each ring after the track's other handles, the arrow keys nudge it, and a run of presses is one step. The rings sit beneath the move, rotate and pivot handles and the shear diamonds, so those keep working as before; where one shares a fix, drag the pivot off it, or Tab to the fix.

docs.title: Or type where it goes
docs.text: Move a fix… (on the outline's menu in VS Code, or Move… in the playground's fix list, or right-click a ring) asks where the fix goes. Type a position in any notation Debrief reads, and the field tells you what it understood, how far and which way that moves the fix, and the speeds it would imply, before you commit.

docs.title: Over the ground, or dead reckoned
docs.text:
Legacy Debrief could plot a track two ways. Over the ground (OTG) puts each fix where it was logged. Dead reckoning (DR) starts from the first fix and places each one after it by the course and speed logged at the fix before, the way a navigator plots a DR track. As each track came in, legacy asked which you wanted, with a checkbox: Use this choice for future track imports. The product owner told us that worked well, because a community tends to stick with one or the other, so we've done the same.

Import a REP file and Debrief asks, track by track: How is NELSON plotted? (1 of 3). Choose over the ground or dead reckoning and, as in legacy, tick Use this choice for future track imports if you'd like Debrief to stop asking. The import's notes say how each track was plotted, and, when your remembered choice was used, how to change it.

VS Code asks in a list. A VS Code list has no check box, so the box is the list's last line, an empty or a ticked circle that says off or on: choose it to tick it, and the list stays open for your answer. That's one question per track, the same with the keyboard, the mouse or a screen reader, rather than a second question after each.

Where that remembered choice lives matters. It's yours, not the plot's: a colleague you send a plot to shouldn't inherit it, and it mustn't change what's in a catalogue. So it is kept with your own Debrief settings (the same file VS Code and the Python services both read), never in a catalogue or a plot file. In VS Code it's an ordinary setting, Debrief: Track import mode (ask, OTG or DR), and Debrief: Ask again whether imported tracks are OTG or DR puts it back to asking; in the playground, Ask again sits under Import. The importer itself is simply told the answer, which is also how an agent says which it wants.

What is the plot's is how each track is plotted: the mode is kept on the track, like its colour, and changing it later (Plot over the ground or by dead reckoning…) is one step. A track plotted by dead reckoning keeps its positions as logged beside the dead-reckoned ones, so switching back puts them back exactly; and the track's line is always the positions as plotted, so any other GeoJSON tool draws what Debrief draws. It's tagged DR beside its name, in the outline and in its label on the map; its line is drawn as any track's.

docs.title: Editing a dead-reckoned track
docs.text:
What does dragging a fix mean on a track plotted by dead reckoning? Its positions aren't data in their own right: they're worked out from where the track starts and each fix's course and speed. The product owner decided that's where edits go. Move the whole track and you move where it starts. Do anything else and you change courses and speeds, and the positions are worked out again: a rotation turns the courses, a stretch scales the speeds, a shear adds one set and drift to every leg (so a straight leg steers exactly the course and speed the map shows, and a leg with a turn in it keeps its turn), and smoothing averages courses and speeds rather than positions.

Drag a single fix and Debrief changes the course and speed of the leg into it, so dead reckoning puts it where you let go, and every fix after it follows, as it must on a DR plot. The map shows that as you drag, the later fixes and their rings moving with the pointer, and says what the leg has become: RED ONE (DR) fix at 11:38:00Z: moving 0.35 nmi 056.5°T; leg into it now 068.8°T 18.3 kn. Let go and the step is named the same way: RED ONE (DR) leg into 11:38:00Z now 068.8°T 18.3 kn. Over the ground nothing changes: only the fix you grab moves.

The same thinking settles jump removal. On a DR track a position can only jump if a logged speed is wild, so Debrief offers the fixes whose logged speed is implausible, and removing one lets the leg before it carry on to the fix after. And the positions, courses and speeds as logged are all kept beside the track, untouched by any edit.

Switching back does lose something, though: if you've moved the track, dragged a fix or turned it while it was plotted by dead reckoning, its fixes, courses and speeds go back to those logged and those changes go. So Debrief asks first, saying what changed (where it starts, or the first course and speed that isn't as logged; comparing courses and speeds is what catches a rotation); it's still one step, and Ctrl+Z brings the changes back.

We checked our dead reckoning against legacy's. Legacy plot files save a DR leg's worked-out positions, and placing each fix from the one before, by that fix's course and speed, along the geodesic, puts every fix of the legacy sample plots back within 0.1 m of them. Those plots aren't asked about at all: they say how each leg was plotted, and come in that way, with a note saying so.

docs.title: For agents
docs.text: The same through the tool service: debrief/edit_track with {"action": "move_fix", "fix_time": …, "distance": …, "bearing": …} (or a position), and {"action": "set_plotting_mode", "plotting_mode": "dr"}, each one step with what was asked in its record (back over the ground after a change made while plotted by dead reckoning is refused, saying why, unless the change says "discard_dr_changes": true); and debrief/import_rep takes the mode for each track.

docs.text: Select RED ONE, zoom in until its fixes have rings, and drag one. Then try Tab and the arrow keys, Move… in Fixes…, or OTG/DR… under Track, below the outline, and drag a fix again to see the fixes after it follow; and import a REP file of your own to be asked how its tracks are plotted:

docs.title: Guides
docs.text:
Three guides keep Debrief consistent as it grows one pull request at a time.

Guide North Star (draft) Owner All guides An analyst who has learned one part of Debrief can predict the rest. Style guide: language Say what an analyst would say: plain British English, glossary terms, never software jargon. Ian Mayo Style guide: theme and UI Look native to VS Code; keep colour for what the data means. Ian Mayo Interaction models Predictable and forgiving: the same gesture does the same thing everywhere, and nothing is silent or irreversible (SUB-21, SUB-28). Ian Mayo Tool-author guide A scientist's first tool should take an afternoon. Ian Mayo

The North Stars are drafts for the team to refine during Phase 0. Owners are provisional until the team is staffed.

docs.title: How the guides grow
docs.text:
• A skeleton first. Each guide's version 0 names every top-level section, including empty ones marked with the phase that will fill them. New material goes into a known place. Material that fits nowhere is flagged at review as either new territory or out of scope.
  • With the feature. A guide is extended in the same pull request as the feature that needs it. The pull-request template asks.
  • Every entry cites what it serves. An entry cites the principle or requirement behind it (for example PRN-08 or CAP-24). An entry that cannot cite one is a warning sign.
  • Read end to end at every phase exit. Each owner reads their guide whole at the end of each phase, and resolves contradictions while they are few.

Automated checks for terminology and theme-token use arrive in Phase 1 (DEV-10).

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
The terms Debrief uses in its interface, tools and documentation. The language section of the style guide says when to use them.

Adapted from DOMAIN_GLOSSARY.md in debrief/debrief-future, itself adapted from legacy Debrief's glossary, and corrected to the SRD. The changes are listed at the end.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
Plot. The unit of analysis: one exercise serial or deployment period, its tracks, annotations, sensor observations and narrative, with the history of every change made to it. Stored as GeoJSON in a STAC catalogue (SUB-05).

Plot file. The one file that holds a plot: its content, its island and its whole history. Send it to a colleague and the history goes with it, undo included; they add it to a catalogue with Add a plot file…. Other GeoJSON tools can read it (SUB-07, SUB-19).

Catalogue. A folder of plots, sources and supporting files, described in STAC. Each catalogue holds data of one protection level (SEC-02).

Source. A file imported into Debrief, such as a REP file or a legacy plot. Debrief never changes a source; a revision arrives as a new source (SUB-10). A catalogue keeps its sources, but they don't travel with a plot file: the plot's first step holds what was imported, and its history names each source.

Supporting file. Video, imagery, acoustic files and other content that is not geographic data, kept beside a plot (SUB-06).

History (in guides, provenance). The record of every operation that produced a plot: imports, tool runs, edits and deletions, with who or what made them (SUB-18 to SUB-24). Kept in the plot file, all of it, always.

Step. One change in a plot's history: what made it, who, when, and what it changed. A step is in the plot, undone (can be redone) or replaced by a later change (kept on record) (SUB-19, SUB-21).

Checksum (in guides). A short fingerprint of some data that changes if the data does. Each step of a plot's history carries one covering the step and the step before, and the current step records the checksum of the plot's content, so a history altered outside Debrief is noticed. The island is outside every checksum (SUB-19).

Time window. The period of the plot being looked at, one for the whole plot. Sensor data is shown only within it (CAP-28, CAP-29). Saved with the plot, but not part of its history: changing it is never undone.

Saved window. The time window as saved in the plot. A tool that moves current time outside it shows a wider or moved window instead, without saving it; the time controller says so, with Keep to save the window shown and Revert to show the saved window again (CAP-28).

Context tracks. Each track's whole line outside the time window, drawn thin and quieter so the whole picture stays in view. A plot draws them visible (at least 3:1 against the map), faint or hidden (CAP-29).

Island (in guides). View state saved inside the plot file, so it travels with the plot, but outside its history: never recorded, never undone. The time window is the first. Everything else in a plot, a track's colour and what is hidden included, is part of its history (SUB-22).

Feature. Anything in a plot: a track, an annotation, or a set of sensor observations. Used where a statement covers all three, as in "Plot features" in the outline; otherwise name the kind.

Fix. A single timestamped position of a platform, with course, speed and depth where known. Depth is positive down.

Track. The movement of one platform over time: its fixes in order.

Annotation. A line, area, circle, ellipse, label, marker, note or period of interest drawn on or attached to a plot, or chart furniture such as the north arrow (CAP-03). An annotation with only a time, such as a note or a period, has no position (CAP-04). How it looks (colour, line, fill, label) is part of the plot: changing it is a step in its history. Write annotation, not shape, in the interface.

Circle, ellipse (annotations). Every position at one range from a centre; or an ellipse about a centre, its longer axis along a true bearing. Ranges are measured along geodesics. Kept in the plot file with their exact centre and size, and a polygon approximating them so other GeoJSON tools see the area (CAP-03).

Handle. A small square or circle on an annotation or a track selected on the map, dragged (or moved with the arrow keys) to change it: a corner, the point between two corners, a centre, a radius, an ellipse's axis end or side; a track's move and rotate handles, its pivot, and the diamonds at its ends, to shear or stretch it. Letting go is one step.

Pivot. The position a track is rotated about. Each fix keeps its range from the pivot; its bearing from the pivot turns. Unless the analyst chooses, the fix nearest current time (CAP-01).

Shear (tracks). Holding one end of a track, or of its fixes in the time window, and dragging the other: every fix moves in proportion to its time from the held end, so a straight leg at a steady speed stays one, with a new course and speed. The drag analysts use most with TMA legs. One step (CAP-01, CAP-21).

Stretch (tracks). Holding one end and dragging the other along the track: every fix keeps its bearing from the held end and its range from it is scaled, so speeds change and courses do not. One step (CAP-01, CAP-21).

Course made good, speed made good. The course and speed of a period of a track taken from its first fix to its last: what a shear or a stretch reports and is given.

Split, merge (tracks). Splitting a track at a time makes two tracks, the fixes before it and the fixes from it on; merging joins tracks into one in time order, and is refused where they overlap in time. Each is one step (CAP-01).

Jump. A fix the platform could not have reached in time from the last good fix before it: faster than a threshold speed, unless the analyst says three times the track's median speed, at least 10 kn. Jumps are found and shown first; those the analyst confirms are removed as one step (CAP-01).

Smoothing. Moving each fix of a track, or of a period of it, to the average position of itself and the same number of fixes either side, the first and last fixes staying where they are. Previewed first; applied as one step (CAP-01).

Marked fix. A fix with a colour, a label or a comment of its own, as legacy plots carry. Found by its time, so the mark stays with its fix whatever else changes. Each change is one step (CAP-01, EXT-14).

Moving a fix (a single fix). Putting one fix of a track somewhere else, alone: its time, its recorded course and speed, and every other fix stay. The speeds its new position implies, to reach it and to go on from it, are said. One step (CAP-01).

OTG, DR (over the ground, dead reckoning). How legacy Debrief plotted a track: OTG, each fix where it was logged; DR, from a start, each fix placed from the one before by the course and speed recorded there. Debrief asks which as each track is imported, unless the analyst said to use one choice for future imports (their setting, which they can clear); the mode is kept on the track, and changing it is one step (CAP-01). On a DR track an edit changes where it starts, or its courses and speeds, and the positions are worked out again; its positions, courses and speeds as logged are kept unchanged beside it (see Track operations).

Fix list. A track's fixes in time order, each with its time, position, course, speed and any mark, for choosing one fix to colour, label or comment on.

Chart furniture. What a chart carries besides its data: the scale bar, always drawn, and the north arrow, which a plot shows or not.

Timeline. The view listing a plot's time-only annotations, such as narrative notes and periods of interest, in time order. Choosing an entry moves current time to it (CAP-05). The SRD calls it the temporal view.

Named set. A saved selection of features, reusable as a selection or as a tool's input (TL-11).

Narrative. The log of events from each platform, imported from Word or PDF and combined on one time axis (CAP-19, CAP-20).

Serial. A period of an exercise, typically 4, 6, 12 or 24 hours.

docs.title: Sensors and TMA
docs.text:
Sensor. A device on a platform that observes others: sonar, radar or visual.

Sensor observations (contacts, cuts). Measurements from a sensor, in Debrief usually bearings. Weeks of them may be held as one set (CON-02).

Bearing. The direction from one position to another, measured clockwise from true north. A relative bearing is measured from the platform's own heading. Debrief displays true bearings as three figures: 045.0°T.

Ambiguous bearing. A towed-array bearing that could be on either side of the array: two candidate bearings mirrored about the array's axis. The analyst resolves each to one side (CAP-22).

Bearing error. The uncertainty of a bearing, where the sensor data supplies it. Debrief can draw such a bearing as a wedge of that width (CAP-22).

TMA (target motion analysis). Estimating a target's course and speed from bearings, typically bearing-only from passive sonar. A solution is rooted in a selected period of bearings, and its positions match the bearing times (CAP-21).

Residual. The difference between a measured bearing and the bearing to the solution at the same time. Small, unpatterned residuals suggest a good solution.

Leg. A period of steady conditions. An ownship leg has steady course and speed; a bearing leg has a steady bearing rate. Changes of ownship leg give the geometry TMA needs.

SATC (semi-automatic track construction). Generating a TMA solution automatically from bearings. Lower priority than manual TMA (CAP-21).

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text:
Tote. The table of relative geometry between one primary and several secondary platforms at current time: range, bearing and other measures (CAP-06).

Measure group. A named, reusable set of measures for a mode of analysis, defined by a study's lead analyst. The Tote is a view onto one (CAP-07).

CPA (closest point of approach). The time and range at which two platforms are nearest.

Current time. The instant, within a time range, that every view follows. Shared state, with selection and viewport (SUB-26).

Display window. The earlier name for the time window, when each layer was to have its own. There is now one time window for the whole plot (CAP-28, decision 12 Oct 2026).

Storyboard. A sequence of map views, each with a time and narrative comments, exported as offline HTML, a PowerPoint quad chart or video (CAP-13, CAP-14).

Tool. An analysis operation written in Python: Debrief builds its form and offers it when it applies (section 6 of the SRD).

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
Time. Stored in UTC to the millisecond (SUB-01) and shown in Zulu time unless the analyst chooses a display zone.

Position. Latitude, positive north, and longitude, positive east, on WGS84. Debrief measures range and bearing along geodesics on the WGS84 ellipsoid, whatever the map's projection (SUB-03). Legacy Debrief used a flat-earth model, so its figures can differ by about 0.4% in range.

Units. Every stored quantity carries its unit. Analysts choose display units: knots, nautical miles, yards, metres, kilometres, degrees (SUB-02, SUB-04).

Direction Degrees Radians North 0° 0 East 90° π/2 South 180° π West 270° 3π/2

docs.title: Changes from the earlier glossary
docs.text: Earlier glossary Now Why Times have microsecond precision Millisecond precision; finer legacy times are truncated on import and the truncation recorded SUB-01, EXT-14 Contacts carry frequency Frequency is not imported; acoustic analysis stays in the acoustic replay application CAP-22, EXT-03 Speeds include feet per second Knots, metres per second, kilometres per hour Schema unit enums Track segments: core, TMA, planning, infill Not yet in the v4 data model; TMA solutions are rooted in a bearing period CAP-21 Depth in every location Positions are latitude and longitude; a track may carry a depth series, positive down Schema 0.0.4 World Location, World Speed, World Distance, World Vector Position, quantities with units Implementation names, not domain terms Plot is a collection of tracks Plot is the unit of analysis, a GeoJSON FeatureCollection in a STAC catalogue SUB-05

docs.title: Sample data
docs.text:
The sample data is a small exercise for demonstrations, walkthroughs and blog posts (DEP-08). It replaces the 1995 single-serial sample. Real, open AIS traffic gives the background picture; on top of it sits an invented exercise: a blue ownship, a red submarine, the ownship's sonar bearings and a scripted narrative, over three serials.

Everything except the AIS is fiction. Use only this data in blog posts and interactive examples (DEV-05, DEV-06).

docs.title: Building it
docs.text:
uv run python -m debrief_sample build sample

This creates a catalogue in the folder sample, with one plot per serial. The same seed, built with the same versions of Debrief's libraries, always gives the same files, byte for byte; --seed gives a different exercise over the same AIS traffic.

docs.title: What is in it
docs.text:
The exercise lies in open water east of the entrance to Chesapeake Bay, on 15 Jun 2023. The area was chosen because open AIS covers it, not for any naval use. It is on the continental shelf, mostly 10 to 35 m deep, so RED ONE's depths are notional.

Serial Time Story 1 08:00Z to 12:00Z BLUE ONE gains RED ONE, classifies it and follows it south-west, losing and regaining it. 2 12:00Z to 17:00Z RED ONE heads west for the shipping lane; BLUE ONE zigzags astern of it to resolve range. 3 17:00Z to 23:00Z BLUE ONE sprints and drifts; RED ONE evades, and is not regained after the first sprint.

Each plot holds:

  • Background traffic. 8 to 10 AIS tracks: merchant ships under way and at anchor, a tug, yachts and pleasure craft. Each is named by its type and a number, such as "Cargo 03", never by its real name.
  • BLUE ONE and RED ONE. One fix a minute. RED ONE's tracks carry depth. Both were written as REP files and imported, so they are sources like any analyst's.
  • Sonar bearings. BLUE ONE's bow sonar on RED ONE every 30 seconds, with a 1.5° error. The sonar can hold RED ONE only within 4.5 nmi, outside its baffles astern and while not sprinting, and within those limits contact comes and goes, so each serial has gaps. Between 177 and 349 bearings per serial, held as one set of sensor observations (CON-02).
  • Narrative. About 35 entries per serial, in Zulu time, from BLUE ONE, RED ONE and exercise control (EXCON): intentions, alterations of course, first contact and its classification, contacts lost and regained, bearing reports with their drift, and closest approaches. The log is kept as a supporting file, and each entry is also a note at its time.
  • The exercise area, as a shape, and two named sets: Exercise and Background traffic.

docs.title: Its history, as a worked example
docs.text:
Every plot records how it was made (SUB-18). Its history names each source with its content hash (SUB-11), and each tool with its version (SUB-24). The steps that use randomness record their seed and how each random generator is derived from it (SUB-20), and the synthesis records a digest of the serial's script, so a replay can tell whether it runs the same script.

flowchart LR
    B["debrief-sample<br/>seed 1995"] --> BR[blue-one.rep]
    B --> RR[red-one.rep]
    BR --> I1["REP import"]
    RR --> I2["REP import"]
    A[AIS extract] --> I3["AIS import"]
    I1 --> S["Sonar bearings<br/>seed 1995"]
    I2 --> S
    S --> P[bearings payload]
    N[narrative.txt] --> I4["Narrative import"]
    B --> AR["Exercise area"]
    B --> NS["Named sets"]
    I1 & I2 & I3 & P & I4 & AR & NS --> Plot[(Plot)]

To see the history of a serial, open its plot.geojson and read provenance. Each source sits in the plot's sources folder, read-only; checking the sources reports nothing when none has changed.

docs.title: The AIS data
docs.text: The background traffic comes from the US national AIS archive, published by NOAA's Office for Coastal Management on MarineCadastre.gov from the US Coast Guard's receiver network. It is a US Government work, in the public domain in the United States. One day was reduced to a small area, the serial windows and 16 vessels, thinned to one fix a minute, with military, law-enforcement, pilot and search-and-rescue vessels left out. Every identifier was removed. The reduction and the licence are described beside the extract, in python/debrief-sample/data/README.md.

docs.title: Not yet in it
docs.text:
• Ambiguous bearings from a towed array (CAP-22): the sonar is a bow sonar, so its bearings are not ambiguous.
  • A narrative as an analyst would import it, from Word or PDF (CAP-19): the log is plain text, and it is a supporting file rather than a source, because the builder wrote it.
  • Labels on fixes: REP labels are not yet imported.

docs.title: Interaction models
docs.text:
North Star: predictable and forgiving: the same gesture does the same thing everywhere, and nothing is silent or irreversible (SUB-21, SUB-28).

Worked patterns applied the same way across hosts, tools and agents (DEV-08). Each model is one short page: the requirements it cites, a Mermaid sequence diagram, and a pointer to its reference implementation. Where an interaction is already a requirement, the model cites it rather than restating it.

Model Written in Status Selection and tool offering Phase 1 Requirements gathered Tool invocation and forms Phase 1 Requirements gathered Unavailable capabilities Phase 1 Requirements gathered Undo Phase 2 Written Conflicts Phase 2 Written Long-running operations Phase 2 Requirements gathered Check overrides Phase 2 Requirements gathered Time controller Phase 3 Written Annotations Phase 3 Written (forms; drawing and editing on the map) Track operations Phase 3 Written (part A: move, rotate, split, merge; part B1: shear, stretch; part B2: jumps, smoothing, marked fixes; part B3: single fixes, dead reckoning) Keyboard equivalents Phase 3 Partly written (annotations, tracks)

Analysts review the Phase 1 models before they are built.

docs.title: Annotations
docs.text: How an analyst adds a line, area, circle, ellipse, label, marker or note to a plot, changes how it looks and when it is shown, deletes it, and finds notes by time. Part A: everything through forms. Part B: drawing annotations on the map, and changing them there by dragging handles or with the keyboard.

docs.title: Requirements cited
docs.text: SRD Requirement CAP-03 Annotations (shapes, labels, chart furniture) are ordinary GeoJSON features, with provenance, export and tool support. CAP-04 An annotation with only a time has no geometry. CAP-05 A temporal view shows narrative entries and time-only annotations. SUB-19, SUB-21 Every change is a recorded step; undo is replay to a point. SUB-22 Content, how features are styled included, is recorded and undoable. SUB-04 Positions, ranges, bearings and times are read and shown in the analyst's notation and units. CAP-28 An annotation with a time or a period is drawn only while it falls in the time window. EXT-14, EXT-15 Legacy plots' annotations come in as far as the data model allows; what doesn't is listed. NFR-13 Every map action, drawing an annotation included, has a keyboard or form-based equivalent. SUB-26, SUB-28 Drawing changes neither current time, the window nor the selection; a change made elsewhere is never overwritten.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
1. Seven kinds, one form. Add annotation… (the + on the Outline view's title bar, or on the Timeline's; Add… under Annotation, below the outline, in the playground) opens the annotation form beside the map. Its Kind is one of:

    Kind Is Positions Line a line through two or more positions, drawn along geodesics one per line Area a closed area with three or more corners one per line Circle every position at one range from a centre the centre, and a radius with its unit Ellipse an ellipse about a centre the centre; semi-major and semi-minor axes with their unit; the longer axis's orientation in degrees true Label text at a position one Marker a marked position one Note text at a time, with no position none: it needs a time

    A new annotation starts as a circle in the middle of the map, with nothing else filled in. The word shape is not used in the interface: shapes are kinds of annotation (style guide, language).

  2. Positions in the analyst's notation. A position may be typed as Debrief writes it (50°20.120'N 004°07.210'W), in degrees, minutes and seconds, in decimal degrees, without the symbols (50 20.12 N 4 7.21 W), with the hemisphere first (N50 20.12 W4 7.21), or as two signed decimals, latitude first (50.335, -4.120). Under each, the form says what it understood (Means 50°20.120'N 004°07.210'W) or what is wrong with it. The same reading runs in Python and TypeScript, held to shared test vectors (schemas/vectors/positions.json), and agents may send positions as text too.

  3. Sizes in their units. A radius or semi-axes is a number and a unit: nautical miles, yards, metres or kilometres. The unit is kept with the value (SUB-02), so a circle of 2 nmi stays 2 nmi when the analyst's display unit is yards. A radius or semi-axis is at most 10,000 km: beyond about half the world, a circle drawn along geodesics folds back on itself. Orientation is degrees true, clockwise from north; 405 is read as 045.

  4. Time. No time (always shown), At a time or Over a period. Times are typed as for a tool's time fields (09:30Z, 15 Jun 2023 09:30:00Z, 150930Z JUN 23), with what was understood said beneath; a new annotation's time starts at current time. With a time or a period, it is drawn only while that falls in the time window (CAP-28). A note always has a time.

  5. Style. Colour (the annotation amber, a track colour by name, or any colour as #rrggbb, its swatch beside the list); line solid, dashed or dotted, and its width in pixels; for areas, circles and ellipses a fill colour and how opaque it is; the label's size in pixels and where it goes (above, below, left, right, centre, or not shown). An area's, a circle's or an ellipse's label is hidden while the shape is too small on screen to carry it: under 70 pixels across where Debrief placed the label, or under 24 where the analyst (or a legacy plot) chose its place. Anything left at its default is drawn as Debrief draws annotations: amber, dashed, an area faintly tinted, so nothing a tool draws is mistaken for a track. An annotation drawn solid still has no direction ticks or end dots, and is still labelled. Style is content: changing it is a step (decision, 12 Oct 2026).

  6. Checked as typed, saved as one step. Each field says what is wrong beside it once the analyst has tried to save; nothing is sent until every field is right. Add (or Save changes) sends the description to the tool service, which checks it again, makes the annotation and records it as one step, named in the History view: Circle 'Exclusion zone' added, Style of Circle 'Exclusion zone' changed, Time of …, … renamed …, Circle 'Exclusion zone' changed (anything else, or several at once). Saving changes that change nothing records nothing: a field left as it was shown keeps its exact value, even where the form shows it rounded (a position to a thousandth of a minute, a time to the second). A field emptied is cleared: text, time and style go back to none. Ctrl+Z undoes it like any step.

  7. Changing one. Its properties form opens from the outline's context menu (Change annotation…), from Change… in the playground, or by double-clicking it on the map. It shows everything the annotation is, in the same fields; its kind stays as it is. A change made elsewhere since the plot was opened is never overwritten: Debrief shows the latest and says nothing was changed (SUB-28).

  8. Deleting. Delete on its form, Delete annotation on the outline's context menu (several at once, as one step), or Delete in the playground. Named sets keep their other members; a set left empty goes too. Undo brings everything back.

  9. Chart furniture. The scale bar is always drawn, in the analyst's distance unit. The north arrow is chart furniture the plot carries: North arrow on the Outline view's ... menu (checked when shown), or the North arrow button in the playground, adds or removes it as a step. The map is Web Mercator, north up everywhere, so the arrow points up. Grids, legends and other furniture are not done.

  10. The Timeline (CAP-05). A view below the outline lists the plot's time-only annotations, such as narrative notes and periods of interest, in time order: each entry its time (or period), name and first line of text. The entry current time is at, the last to start at or before it, is marked; in VS Code the view keeps it in sight as current time moves, so a narrative can be read along with a replay. Choosing an entry (click, or Enter) moves current time to it, or to its start. If that is outside the window shown, the window widens or moves to take it in, shown but never saved, exactly as for a tool's time, with Keep and Revert on the time controller (CAP-28). It is a native tree in VS Code, read by screen readers and used from the keyboard like any view; in the playground, a list of buttons, the current one marked for screen readers as well as by sight.

  11. What is a step, and what isn't.

    Step in the history Undone by Ctrl+Z Adding, changing, restyling, deleting an annotation Yes, one each Yes Drawing on the map: placing points, cancelling No: the step is Add on the form that follows No Letting go of a handle, or a run of arrow keys on one Yes, one each Yes Showing or removing the north arrow Yes Yes Hiding an annotation on the map Yes (as for any feature) Yes Choosing a Timeline entry (current time), opening a form No No

  12. Drawing on the map. The map has a toolbar, Draw an annotation, below the zoom buttons: Line, Area, Circle, Ellipse, Label, Marker and Cancel. Choosing a kind starts drawing it: the button shows pressed, the map gets a focus outline and a cross for a pointer, and a note at the top of the map says what to do next and what has been drawn so far. Choosing the pressed kind again, Cancel (which leaves the keyboard on that kind) or Escape stops and keeps nothing; Backspace removes the last point placed.

    Kind Draw it by The map says Line clicking each position; double-click or Enter finishes positions placed, the leg to the pointer, range and bearing from the start, length Area clicking each corner; double-click or Enter finishes corners placed, the leg, range and bearing from the start, the area Circle clicking the centre, then the radius; or dragging from the centre radius, its bearing, the area Ellipse clicking the centre, the end of the longer axis (which sets the orientation), then the side (the width); or dragging from the centre to the axis end semi-major, semi-minor, orientation, the area Label, marker one click the position

    Ranges and bearings are along geodesics and in the analyst's units and notation (4.25 nmi 045.0°T); an area is in the square of the length unit (12.30 nmi²). A double-click places one point, not two. A line needs two different positions and an area three; finishing too soon says so and keeps drawing. A circle's radius and an ellipse's axes are kept in the analyst's length unit, to the decimals the map showed, so what is saved is what was read; an ellipse's side can never make the shorter axis the longer. While drawing, a click on a track places a point there; Ctrl or Cmd click still selects. Drawing never changes current time, the window or the selection.

  13. Finishing opens the form. A finished drawing opens the annotation form (Add annotation), with its kind, positions and size filled in, at the name. The analyst names it, gives it a time or a style if they want, and Add saves it as one step (Area 'Patrol box' added); Cancel (or closing the form) keeps nothing, and the dashed drawing leaves the map. Until then nothing is in the plot. Why the form, rather than adding at once with a made-up name: adding at once and then naming it would be two steps for one annotation, and Undo would take away only the name; a made-up name ("Area 1") would end up in plots. With the form, each finished annotation is one undoable step with the analyst's own name, and Cancel leaves no trace in the history.

  14. Changing it on the map. An annotation selected on its own, and drawn on the map now, shows handles in the theme's focus colour, and the note at the top says how to use them (on a map narrower than 480 pixels the note gives way to the map; each handle's own name says it):

    Kind Handles Line, area one at each position or corner; a smaller, dashed one between each pair (an area's closing side too); a filled one in the middle that moves it all Circle its centre (moves it); its radius Ellipse its centre (moves it); the end of its longer axis (length and orientation); its side (width) Label, marker its position

    Dragging a handle changes the annotation as the pointer moves, saying what it now measures; letting go saves the change as one step, named for what was done: Circle 'Keep clear' moved, Circle 'Keep clear' resized, Area 'Patrol box' reshaped (a corner moved, added or removed, or an ellipse's axes), Area 'Patrol box' moved (all of it). Escape during a drag puts it back, and nothing is recorded. Dragging a between-handle adds a corner (or position) there. Moving a whole line or area moves every corner by the same change of latitude and longitude, as a parallel rule would on a chart. Sizes keep their own units: a circle of 4 km stays in km.

  15. The keyboard. Every drawing and every change can be made without a pointer:

    • Drawing: Tab to the toolbar and press Enter on a kind; the keyboard goes to the map, which shows a cross in its middle. The arrow keys pan the map under the cross (as they always do), Space places a point at the cross, Enter finishes, Backspace removes the last point, Escape cancels.
    • Changing: Tab to a handle (each is named for a screen reader: Area 'Patrol box': corner 2 of 4; drag it, or use the arrow keys; Delete removes it). The arrow keys move it 5 pixels, 25 with Shift; a run of presses is saved as one step once they stop (under a second), on Enter, or when the keyboard moves on; Escape first puts it back. Presses made while that step is still being saved are not lost: the map says so, and they are made as the next step once it is. Arrow keys on a between-handle add a corner there. Delete or Backspace on a corner removes it, unless that would leave an area fewer than three corners or a line fewer than two, which the map says.
    • Exactly: the properties form (item 7) changes any position or size by typing it, as before.

  16. Shared state and conflicts. Drawing and editing change neither current time, the time window nor the selection; tracks stay selectable with Ctrl or Cmd click. If the plot changes elsewhere during a drag (a colleague, an agent), the map shows the latest at once, drops the drag and says The plot was changed elsewhere, so your change was not made. Debrief is showing the latest; try again if you still want to. A change sent from a plot that has since moved on is refused the same way (SUB-28). A change the service refuses for any other reason is said in a notification, and the map shows the annotation as it is.

  17. For agents. The same steps through the tool service: debrief/add_annotation (annotation: the description the form sends, positions as numbers or text), debrief/edit_annotation (feature, and annotation with only what changes, so {"appearance": {...}} restyles; a member given as null is cleared, and a time given replaces a period, or a period a time; the north arrow has nothing to change), debrief/delete_annotations (features) and debrief/set_north_arrow (shown), each with base as for any change. In VS Code the commands debrief.addAnnotation, debrief.editAnnotation, debrief.deleteAnnotation, debrief.toggleNorthArrow and debrief.goToTime take the same arguments instead of opening the form.

    participant Map

    Map->>Map: sketch, with range, bearing and area as it goes

docs.title: How circles and ellipses are kept
docs.text: GeoJSON has no curves. A circle or an ellipse is kept as a polygon of 72 sides approximating it, built along geodesics, as its geometry, so that any other GeoJSON tool draws the area it covers and a plot's extent includes it, plus its own properties: shape (circle or ellipse), centre, and radius, or semi_major, semi_minor and orientation, each with its unit. Debrief draws and edits it from those, along geodesics and smooth at any zoom, never from the polygon; every change makes the polygon again, and a rule checked on reading refuses a polygon that no longer matches its centre and size. A point with a radius would have been smaller, but other tools would see only a point, and a plot's extent would leave the circle out.

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text: What happens when a plot changes on disk while an analyst has it open.

docs.title: Requirements cited
docs.text: SRD Requirement SUB-28 Debrief detects the change and never silently overwrites it. SUB-29 Offer to save as a new plot; offer to merge non-overlapping changes by replaying deltas; never merge overlapping changes automatically; never lock files. SUB-14, SUB-35 Refuse newer-schema files; warn before writing a newer-schema file into a shared catalogue. NFR-11 Saves are atomic; a failed save leaves the original intact and says so. SUB-19 The plot's whole history is in its plot file, protected by checksums.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
Plots are never locked (SUB-29). Instead every change says which version of the plot it was made against (its base), and is refused if the plot has moved on.

  1. Noticed while open. Debrief checks each second whether the open plot's file has changed on disk: another window, another analyst on a shared folder, an agent. The plot file holds the plot's whole history, so Debrief compares the history's current step, how many steps it holds, and the checksum of the content the current step recorded. If the plot has moved on, the map, outline and History view show the latest, and a notification says "Serial 1 was changed elsewhere. Debrief is showing the latest." (SUB-28). Nothing the analyst had done is lost: their changes were already saved as steps. If only the plot's time window changed (its island), Debrief shows the new window and says so, without reading the plot again.
  2. Met by a tool run. If the plot changed between the analyst opening it and running a tool, the tool's result is not saved. Debrief asks, in a dialog:
  3. where the two changes touch different features: Combine the changes (the tool's result is applied on top of the other change) or Save mine as a new plot;
  4. where they touch the same features (including a named set that refers to a feature the other change deleted): only Save mine as a new plot. Overlapping changes are never combined automatically.
  5. Cancel saves nothing and shows the latest; the analyst can run the tool again.
  6. Saved as a new plot. The new plot, Serial 1 (your changes), has the history the analyst was working from (every step up to it, unchanged, checksums and all), the same sources and files, and then their change. The original keeps the other change. Debrief offers to open it.
  7. Met by undo. Undo is refused if the plot changed since it was shown; Debrief shows the latest and says nothing was undone.

  8. Newer schema. A plot written by a newer Debrief is refused, with the version it needs, and never partly loaded (SUB-14). Before saving a change, an undo or an import would write a newer schema into a catalogue other analysts share, Debrief says so and asks: Save anyway updates the catalogue's declared version; closing the dialog saves nothing (SUB-35). Until schema 1.0 a catalogue must match exactly to open at all (SUB-13), so the question first appears after 1.0.

  9. Changed outside Debrief. A plot whose history fails its checksums (a step altered, removed or moved by hand) is shown as its file holds it, but Debrief changes nothing in it and says so: "This plot's history has been changed outside Debrief: step 2 of its history is not as Debrief recorded it. Debrief shows the plot as its file holds it, but will not change it. Ask whoever sent it for a fresh copy." A plot whose content no longer matches its intact history (edited in another program, say) is rebuilt from its history, the file as found is kept beside it, and Debrief says so. A change to the time window alone is never treated as either.

Each save rewrites the whole plot file, content and history together, through a new file that replaces the old one only once it is complete, and takes a lock for the milliseconds it lasts, so two processes saving at once can't interleave; a reader never waits (NFR-11). If a process dies part-way, the plot file is the one from before that save, whole; opening the plot says a save was interrupted.

    participant History as Plot history

    Analyst->>Host: Run closest approach
    Host->>Service: tools/call (base: step 4)
    Service->>History: commit (base step 4)
    History-->>Service: Conflict (mergeable: different features)
    Service-->>Host: isError, _meta debrief/conflict

    Analyst->>Host: Combine the changes

docs.title: Selection and tool offering
docs.text:
How an analyst selects features, in the map, outline or catalogue, and how Debrief offers the tools that apply to that selection.

The model, its sequence diagram and its reference implementation are written in Phase 1. Version 0 gathers the requirements it must satisfy.

docs.title: Requirements cited
docs.text: SRD Requirement SUB-26, SUB-27 Selection is shared state that views, extensions and tools can all read and set. TL-06 Each tool declares the feature types it applies to. TL-08 The tools offered are those that apply to every selected item. TL-09 A tool declaring an unknown type is not offered, and Debrief says why. TL-11 Named sets are reusable as a selection. NFR-13 Selection is possible by keyboard.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
One selection, everywhere. The analyst selects features in the map or the outline, and every view shows the same selection (SUB-26).

Gesture Map Outline Select one feature Click it Click it Add or remove one Ctrl click (Cmd on macOS) Ctrl click (Cmd on macOS) Select a range — Shift click Clear Escape, or click empty sea Clear selection (the button in the outline's title bar) Zoom to the selection Selected button, top left —

Ctrl or Cmd adds in both places, as everywhere in VS Code. Shift selects a range in the outline, and does nothing on the map, which has no order to make a range of.

  • Showing selection.
  • On the map. Each selected feature gets a dotted outline in the theme's text colour. That colour is never a force colour, so selecting tracks never makes them look blue or red. Everything else is dimmed.
  • In the outline. Selected features are marked selected. The last one selected elsewhere is revealed and highlighted.
  • In the tools view. The selection is counted.
  • Offering tools. Whenever the selection changes, the tools view asks the tool service which tools apply to every selected item, within each tool's count limits (TL-08). The rule lives in Python, so agents get the same answer (TL-14).
  • Explaining tools not on offer. Tools that don't apply are listed under Other tools, each saying what it needs ("select 2 tracks"), rather than being hidden (CON-10).
  • Unknown data types. Tools that name a data type Debrief doesn't know appear under Not available, with the reason (TL-09).
  • Time-only annotations. These have no position, so they appear only in the outline (CAP-04).

docs.title: Time controller
docs.text: How an analyst sets the plot's time window and current time, plays through them, and what is saved where.

docs.title: Requirements cited
docs.text: SRD Requirement CAP-28 One time window for the whole plot, independent of its overall time range, saved in the plot file as view state. A tool's time outside it is shown, never saved, until the analyst keeps or reverts it. CAP-29 Tracks for a whole deployment at once, at least 3:1 against the map outside the window by default; sensor data only within the window. SUB-22 View state in the island is neither undoable nor recorded; two analysts changing it at once are told, not overwritten. SUB-26, SUB-27 Current time (an instant and a range) is shared state that views, extensions and tools read and set. SUB-28 A change made elsewhere is never silently overwritten. NFR-13 Everything works from the keyboard, in any theme.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
1. One controller, every host. VS Code shows it as the Time view at the top of the Debrief sidebar, above the catalogues, outline, tools and history. The playground shows the same component at the top of its side column. The map only draws: it has no control of its own.

    The controller is compact, so the whole of it shows without scrolling at the height VS Code first gives the view (at 1440 × 900, with the other Debrief views open), note and all. From the top: the window's start and end, with its length, on one line; the window's slider; the note, when there is one, on one line; current time's slider, with the step beside it; and ‹, ▶, ›, the speed and current time on one line. Names that a caption would repeat are on hover and for screen readers instead. 2. The time window is a slider with two handles over the plot's whole period. Drag a handle to move that end; drag the band between them to move the whole window. Above it, the window's start and end, and how long it is. The window is never shorter than one second: the handles stop a second apart and never cross. A plot saved with a window of no length opens showing its first second, and that is saved only if the analyst moves it. 3. Current time is a slider over the window, never outside it. When the window moves past current time, current time moves with it. ‹ and › step back and forward; the step, about a hundredth of the window (1 s up to 1 day), shows beside the slider. Current time itself shows at the end of the buttons' line. 4. Play (▶, or Space) moves current time forward at the chosen speed and stops at the end of the window. Playing from the end starts again at the window's start. The speeds are multiples of real time:

    Speed Plays For 1× real time a close-quarters encounter, second by second 10× ten minutes a minute an approach 60× (the default) a minute a second a four-hour serial in four minutes 600× ten minutes a second a serial in under half a minute 3600× an hour a second a week's deployment in under three minutes

    Current time moves ten times a second while playing: smooth to follow, without flooding the views. A window shorter than one of those moves (the speed times a tenth of a second: 6 s at 60×) cannot be played: Play is off and says Window too short to play at 60×: widen it or slow down, on hover and to screen readers. It stays focusable, so the reason can be read.

  2. What the map shows. Within the window, tracks are drawn in full: solid lines 2.5 px wide, direction ticks, a hollow dot at the first fix in the window and a filled, labelled dot at the last. Outside it, each whole track stays in view as a context track, so a deployment of weeks still reads as one picture (CAP-29): a solid line 1.5 px wide, with no ticks, dots or labels, in the track's hue made quieter (moved toward the theme's text colour). Annotations with a time or a period are drawn only while it falls in the window; annotations without one always are. Sensor data will be drawn only within the window (CAP-29); bearings are not drawn yet.

    Context tracks are set for the plot and saved in its island like the window. In VS Code they are in the Time view's ... menu, on its title bar: Context tracks: Visible, Faint and Hidden, the plot's choice checked (the commands debrief.contextTracks.visible, .faint and .hidden, which run debrief.setContextTracks). When the analyst's setting draws faint as visible, the view's title says so. The playground has no title menu: its Context list is beside the window's length.

    Setting Draws them Visible (the default) At least 3:1 against the map's background on any theme, as drawn. Debrief works this out from the theme's editor background: opacity 0.6, and each colour's lightness moved away from the background only as far as it needs. Faint Fainter (opacity 0.35), for a busy plot. No 3:1 promise. Hidden Not at all: only the window shows.

    An analyst who needs the contrast everywhere turns on the setting Debrief › Map: Minimum Context Contrast (debrief.map.minimumContextContrast): faint is then drawn visible on every plot they open, without changing the plot; hidden is still hidden. High-contrast themes draw context tracks in the track's own colour, opaque, 1 px wide. Selecting a feature dims the others, context tracks included, but never below opacity 0.3, and never on a high-contrast theme. 6. Moving shows; letting go saves. The map follows the window as it moves. The window is saved in the plot when the analyst lets go: the pointer is released, or the key is released. Holding an arrow key down saves once. Saving on every movement would rewrite the plot file many times a second and, on a shared folder, look to a colleague like a flood of changes. 7. What is saved where.

    Where Undoable In the history Time window, context tracks The plot file, in its island No No Current time Shared state, not saved No No Colour, hiding, data The plot, through its history Yes Yes

    The window travels with the plot: a colleague given the plot file opens it on the same window. Ctrl+Z never changes the window, and moving the window never conflicts with a change to the plot's content. 8. Shared state follows the window. The range of current time in shared state is the window as shown, so tools and other extensions see it, and it follows a drag at once. 9. A tool's time outside the saved window. Closest approach, say, moves current time to the moment it finds. If that is outside the saved window, Debrief shows it without saving anything:

    • the window shown widens by the least amount that takes the time in, but never to more than twice the saved window's length. Beyond that, the window moves instead: the saved length, centred on the time, kept within the plot's period;
    • the part of the window bar that differs from the saved window is hatched, and a note says Showing beyond saved window (or Showing a different period from the saved window, when it moved), with Keep and Revert at its right. The note is one line: in a narrow view its text is cut short, and shows whole on hover. It stays until the analyst chooses, and screen readers hear all of it (a polite live region);
    • the tool's message adds (outside your saved window). The history records the tool's run and its result, such as the closest approach's time, never a window.

    Keep saves the window shown, as letting go does, conflict checks included (SUB-28). Revert shows the saved window again, with current time moved to its nearest edge. Dragging a handle or the band, or moving a handle from the keyboard, saves the window as left, so it counts as Keep. Moving current time, stepping and playing inside the window shown neither save it nor clear the note. If the plot is closed or VS Code reloads, the window shown is lost and the saved one returns.

    A tool whose purpose is to set the window (none ships yet) can ask for its range to be saved (save_window on its state_change). Debrief saves it, through the same path, only when the analyst ran that tool by hand from its form on the plot still open; a run by an agent, a command, a chain or a replay is shown as above, never saved. 10. A colleague's window. If someone else changes the plot's window, Debrief notices (it watches the plot file as well as its history), shows the new window without reading the plot's content again, and says so. If the analyst lets go of a window after a colleague changed it, theirs is kept: Debrief shows it and says Someone else changed the time window, so yours was not saved. Nothing is merged or overwritten silently (SUB-28).

docs.title: Tool invocation and forms
docs.text:
How an analyst runs a tool: the generated parameter form, its explanation, running it, and where the result goes.

The model, its sequence diagram and its reference implementation are written in Phase 1. Version 0 gathers the requirements it must satisfy.

docs.title: Requirements cited
docs.text: SRD Requirement TL-07 Debrief generates the parameter form from the tool's declaration. CAP-24 The form shows the tool's explanation, and any judgement it involves. SUB-04 Values on the form use the analyst's units and notation. TL-11, TL-13 Results may be features, changes, deletions, non-spatial results, named sets or changes to shared state; non-spatial results appear in a temporary panel and can be saved. TL-14 Agents invoke the same tools with the same permissions. SUB-19, SUB-24 Every run is recorded, with the tool's version.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
1. Choose. The analyst picks a tool under For this selection.
  2. Form. The tool's form opens beside the map. Debrief builds it from the declaration (TL-07):
  3. the title and explanation, then any judgement, set apart so it is read (CAP-24);
  4. what the tool will act on ("Applies to: NELSON, BLUE");
  5. one field per parameter, with its explanation and default. A quantity has a unit picker, starting at the default's unit (SUB-04).
  6. Times are typed as the language guide writes them: 09:30Z (on the plot's day), 15 Jun 2023 09:30:00Z, a date-time group such as 150930Z JUN 23, or ISO. Under the field the form says what it understood ("Means 15 Jun 2023 09:30:00Z"), so a mistaken day is caught before the run.
  7. Run. Run sends the values; Cancel closes the form and changes nothing. While the tool runs, the form shows Running… and can't be sent twice.
  8. Refused. If a value is wrong, or the tool fails, the form stays open with the reason above the buttons, in the analyst's words. The plot is untouched (TL-03).
  9. Done. The form closes.
  10. Features. New or changed features appear on the map and in the outline at once. A notification says what changed ("Range rings added 3 features").
  11. Numbers and tables. These open in a Results panel beside the map (TL-13). The panel:
    • repeats the tool's judgement, so a figure is never read without its caveat (CAP-24);
    • says what was added to the plot;
    • says that the figures themselves are not saved;
    • offers Copy for each table, as tab-separated text for a report or spreadsheet.
  12. History. Every run that changes the plot is recorded with the tool, its version, who ran it, the selection and every value (SUB-19, SUB-24). A run that only returns a number or table changes nothing and records nothing.

Agents and keyboard users run the same tools through the Run tool command, without the form. The checks and the records are the same (TL-14).

docs.title: Track operations
docs.text: How an analyst moves a track, or a period of it, rotates it about a point, shears or stretches it from one end, splits it at a time and merges tracks into one; and how they clean it: removing jumps, smoothing it, and giving single fixes a colour, a label or a comment of their own. Part A: moving, rotating, splitting and merging (decision, product owner, 13 Oct 2026). Part B1: shearing and stretching, shear first as the operation analysts use most with TMA legs (decision, product owner, 13 Oct 2026; see Shearing and stretching). Cleaning tracks (part B2, 14 Oct 2026): jump removal, smoothing and marked fixes. Single fixes, and dead reckoning (part B3, 14 Oct 2026): one fix dragged on its own, and the legacy OTG and DR modes, asked of each track imported. Editing a track plotted by dead reckoning (decision, product owner, 14 Oct 2026): every operation on a DR track changes where it starts, or its courses and speeds, and the positions are worked out again.

docs.title: Requirements cited
docs.text: SRD Requirement CAP-01 Dragging, splitting, merging, jump removal and smoothing of tracks; single fixes dragged on their own; the legacy OTG and DR modes. CAP-02 Track edits are destructive in the working plot, each recorded as a delta. CAP-21 The TMA module's manual dragging of a solution: translate, rotate, stretch, shear. SUB-19, SUB-21 Every change is a recorded step; undo is replay to a point, never an inverse operation. SUB-24 Provenance records who made each change, and what they asked for. SUB-03, SUB-04 Measured along geodesics; read and shown in the analyst's units and notation. SUB-26, SUB-28 Moving a track changes neither current time, the window nor the selection; a change made elsewhere is never overwritten. NFR-13 Dragging a track has a keyboard and a form-based equivalent. PRN-08 The analyst owns the data: a track is moved where the analyst says, without second-guessing; nothing is removed or moved without the analyst seeing it first. EXT-14, EXT-15 A legacy plot's per-fix colours, labels and comments are imported, not listed as left out; a leg it plotted by dead reckoning is said to be.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
1. What moves: the whole track, or a period of it. Legacy Debrief dragged a whole track, or a selected time period of it, to line it up with a reference: that is kept (decision, 13 Oct 2026). On the map, a small control below the drawing toolbar, What changes, says which (for moving, rotating, shearing and stretching alike): Whole track (the default) or Time window, the fixes in the time window shown. The forms offer the same choice. An agent may give any period. Fixes whose times fall in the period, ends included, move; the rest stay where they are.

  2. The joins jump. Moving a period moves only its fixes, so the track jumps where they meet the rest: the track is not stretched or smoothed to keep it continuous. (That is over the ground. On a track plotted by dead reckoning the fixes after follow on, with no jump: see Editing a track plotted by dead reckoning.) The map shows the jump while the analyst drags, and says so: only the fixes in the time window move, so the track jumps where they meet the rest. Jump removal (part B) will tidy a join an analyst does not want.

  3. Moving is geodesic. A move takes every fix the same range along the same true bearing, each along its own geodesic, as legacy Debrief offset each fix: not a change of latitude and longitude, as an annotation's whole-shape move is. Courses and speeds over ground are kept as they were. On a curved earth no move of every fix by the same range and bearing keeps a track's shape exactly: as meridians converge, a track far north moved north is squeezed east-west a little, and one moved east turns a little. For the moves an analyst makes the difference is small (a track at 60°N moved 5 nmi north is 0.25% shorter; at 70°N moved 20 nmi, 1.6% shorter; a track steering 000 at 70°N moved 20 nmi east then steers 000.9), so the recorded speeds and courses are kept rather than worked out again from the moved positions.

  4. Rotating is geodesic. A rotation keeps each fix's range from the pivot and turns its bearing from the pivot by the angle; clockwise is positive. Courses over ground of the fixes turned turn with the track: by the angle, near the pivot; far from it, or far north, by a little more or less, as the meridians converge, so that each course is still the track's direction as drawn (turned about the North Pole, a ship steering 090 still steers 090). The pivot is, unless the analyst chooses, the fix nearest current time, when current time is within what moves; otherwise the first fix of what moves. On the map the pivot is a handle of its own: drag it (or move it with the arrow keys) to turn about somewhere else. Moving the pivot records nothing; it says where the next rotation turns about.

  5. Handles. A track selected on its own, and drawn on the map, shows three handles in the theme's focus colour, each named for a screen reader:

    Handle Looks like Does Move a filled square on a fix in the middle of what moves drag it, and the track follows it Rotate a ring beyond the fix farthest from the pivot, on a dashed arm from it drag it round the pivot, and the track turns with it Pivot a dotted ring, by default on the fix nearest current time drag it to choose where the track turns about Ends a diamond beside the first fix and one beside the last fix of what moves (a double edge when Stretch is chosen) drag one to shear the track, or stretch it, holding the other end (below)

    Dragging the move or rotate handle draws the track moved or turned as the pointer goes, the track as it was dashed beneath it, and the note at the top of the map says by how much: BLUE ONE: moving 1.20 nmi 045.0°T, BLUE ONE: rotating 12.0° clockwise about 50°20.120'N 004°07.210'W. Letting go saves it as one step. Escape before letting go puts it back, and nothing is recorded. What is saved is what the note said: the distance in the analyst's length unit and the bearing or angle, each to the decimals shown.

  6. Steps, named for what was done. Each operation is one step in the History view, its first note naming it and later notes saying the rest:

    Operation Named Further notes Move the whole track BLUE ONE moved 1.20 nmi 045.0°T Move a period BLUE ONE part moved 1.20 nmi 045.0°T Only the fixes from 09:30:00Z to 10:15:00Z Rotate BLUE ONE rotated 12.0° clockwise (or part rotated) About 50°20.120'N 004°07.210'W, and the period Split BLUE ONE split at 09:30:00Z Into BLUE ONE (1) and BLUE ONE (2) Merge BLUE ONE and BLUE TWO merged (or 3 tracks merged) Into BLUE ONE, and any series not kept Shear BLUE ONE sheared: 087.2°T 12.4 kn (or part sheared) Held at the start, 09:30:00Z, Was 090.0°T 10.0 kn, and the period Stretch BLUE ONE stretched: 12.4 kn (or part stretched) Held at the end, 10:15:00Z, Was 10.0 kn, and the period

    Each step's provenance record holds who made it, the track or tracks it chose (selected), and what was asked (parameters): the distance and bearing, or the angle and the pivot's latitude and longitude, the period's start and end, the time of a split and the names of its parts, or the merged track's name (SUB-24). Undo is replay to the step before, as for any step (SUB-21).

  7. Splitting at a time. Split track at current time… splits the selected track at current time into two: the fixes before it, and the fixes from it on (a fix exactly at the time starts the second part). The parts are offered as BLUE ONE (1) and BLUE ONE (2), which the analyst may change. Each keeps the track's colour, platform class, hiding and provenance. The first keeps the track's identity, so a named set or a tool result that refers to the track still does; the second is a new track, listed straight after it, and named sets that held the track hold both. Sensor observations that start at or after the time go with the second part. Observations that run across the time are not cut in two: they stay with the first part, and the step's notes say so (2087 bearings runs past the split and stays with BLUE ONE (1)), since those after the time now have a host track that has ended. Each part needs at least two fixes, or nothing is split and the message says how many each side has. Both parts are selected afterwards.

  8. Merging. Merge selected tracks joins two or more selected tracks into one, in time order, whatever order they were selected in. The merged track keeps the earliest's identity, colour and platform class, and is named as the analyst says: offered the earliest's name, or, for the parts of one split track (BLUE ONE (1) and BLUE ONE (2)), the track's own (BLUE ONE); the others go, and sensor observations and named sets that referred to them refer to it. Tracks that overlap in time are not merged, and the message says where: The tracks were not merged: they overlap in time (BLUE ONE and RED ONE from 09:00:00Z to 09:40:00Z). Split or move one so they no longer overlap, then merge them. (Choosing which track wins where they overlap was considered and left out, to keep merging predictable.) Tracks that only meet, one ending as the next starts, merge. Speeds, courses or depths are kept only if every track has them. Before merging tracks where some have none, Debrief asks (Merging BLUE ONE, BLUE TWO keeps only what every track has. Courses not kept: BLUE TWO had none. Undo puts them back., with Merge anyway); the step's notes say which were not kept, and why, and the tool service returns the same in notes. The merged track is selected afterwards.

  9. What is a step, and what isn't.

    Step in the history Undone by Ctrl+Z Letting go of the move or rotate handle Yes, one Yes A run of arrow keys on the move or rotate handle Yes, one for the run Yes Letting go of an end, to shear or stretch Yes, one Yes A run of arrow keys on an end Yes, one for the run Yes Move…, Rotate…, Shear…, Stretch…, Split…, Merge Yes, one each Yes Dragging or nudging the pivot No No Choosing Whole track or Time window, or Shear or Stretch No No Escape during a drag; a move of nothing No No

  10. The keyboard. Tab to a handle. On the move handle the arrow keys move it 5 pixels, 25 with Shift; on the rotate handle Right and Up turn it 1° clockwise, Left and Down 1° anticlockwise, 10° with Shift; on the pivot the arrow keys move it 5 pixels (25 with Shift). A run of presses on the move or rotate handle is saved as one step once they stop (under a second), on Enter, or when the keyboard moves on; Escape first puts it back. Presses made while that step is being saved are not lost: they are made as the next step. Whole track and Time window are buttons on the map, reached with Tab, as are Shear and Stretch. The ends are described below.

  11. The forms. For an exact change, or without the map:

    • Move track… (the outline's context menu on a track; Move… under Track, below the outline, in the playground): what moves (Whole track or Current time window, with how many fixes it holds), the distance (1.2 nmi, 2000 yd, 3 km, or a number in the analyst's unit) and the bearing in degrees true (045). Each field says what it understood (Means 1.20 nmi) or what is wrong.
    • Rotate track…: what turns; the pivot (Fix nearest current time, First fix, Last fix, or in VS Code a position typed in any notation Debrief reads); and the angle (12, 12 clockwise, -12 or 12 anticlockwise).
    • Split track at current time…: the names of the two parts, offered as X (1) and X (2).
    • Merge selected tracks: the merged track's name, offered as above; first, if speeds, courses or depths would not be kept, whether to merge anyway.
    • Shear track… and Stretch track…: below.

  12. Shared state and conflicts. Moving, rotating, splitting and merging change neither current time nor the time window. The selection is kept, except that a split selects both parts and a merge the merged track. If the plot changes elsewhere during a drag (a colleague, an agent), the map shows the latest at once, drops the drag and says The plot was changed elsewhere, so your change was not made. Debrief is showing the latest; try again if you still want to. A change sent from a plot that has since moved on is refused the same way (SUB-28): track operations are never merged with a change made meanwhile. Context tracks follow the track: the whole moved track is drawn as context outside the window. A hidden track is not drawn, so it has no handles, but it can still be moved, rotated, split and merged from the outline.

  13. For agents. The same steps through the tool service: debrief/edit_track (feature, edit: a TrackEdit, {"action": "move", "distance": {"value": 1.2, "unit": "[nmi_i]"}, "bearing": {"value": 45, "unit": "deg"}} or {"action": "rotate", "angle": {"value": -10, "unit": "deg"}, "pivot": [-4.12, 50.33]}, with a period to move or turn only that; for a rotation with no pivot, current_time chooses the default), debrief/split_track (feature, at, and names if wanted) and debrief/merge_tracks (features, and name if wanted), each with base as for any change. Shears and stretches go through debrief/edit_track too (below). In VS Code the commands debrief.moveTrack, debrief.rotateTrack, debrief.shearTrack and debrief.stretchTrack take the track and the edit, debrief.splitTrack the track and {at, names}, and debrief.mergeTracks the tracks' ids and {name}, instead of asking.

sequenceDiagram
    actor Analyst
    participant Map
    participant Host as Extension host
    participant Service as Tool service
    participant Plot as Plot file
    Analyst->>Map: select BLUE ONE
    Map->>Map: move, rotate and pivot handles
    Analyst->>Map: drag the move handle
    Map->>Map: draw the track moved (geodesic), the old one dashed; "moving 1.20 nmi 045.0°T"
    Analyst->>Map: let go

    else

sequenceDiagram
