docs.title: Shearing and stretching
docs.text:
Part B1 (decision, product owner, 13 Oct 2026): shear is the operation analysts use most when working with TMA legs, so it comes first, with stretch beside it. A target's leg is a straight line run at a steady speed; the analyst keeps one end where the bearings put it and changes the course and speed of the rest. Both are legacy Debrief's TMA drags (CAP-21), here on any track.

  1. One end is held. What changes is the whole track or only its fixes in the time window, chosen with the same Whole track and Time window control. One end of it, its first fix or its last, is held (the anchor) and does not move; the analyst drags the other end. Dragging the end at the start holds the end, and the other way round.

  2. Shear: every fix moves in proportion to its time from the held end. Say the held fix is A, at time tA, and the dragged end E, at time tE, is dragged to E′. A fix at time t moves by the fraction f = (t − tA) / (tE − tA) of the end's move: not at all at the held end, the whole of it at the dragged end, half of it halfway in time. A straight leg at a steady speed stays a straight leg at a steady speed, with a new course and a new speed: they change together, as in legacy Debrief's TMA shear.

    A, held E E′ ⅓ of the move ⅔

    Dashed: the leg as it was. Solid: sheared. Each fix moves the part of E's move that its time is of the leg's.

  3. Measured on the earth, from the held end. The move is taken in the frame centred on the held fix in which each position is placed by its range and true bearing from it (an azimuthal equidistant projection): there, a geodesic through the held fix is a straight line, and ranges from it are exact. So a straight leg through the held end (a geodesic, run at a steady speed) stays exactly straight after a shear, at any latitude and across the antimeridian. We considered moving each fix the fraction f of the end's range along the end's bearing, as a move does; but over a leg the meridians close in, the same bearing points slightly differently at each fix, and the sheared leg would bend (by tens of metres over a 10 nmi leg at 50° north). The tests check legs at 50°N, at 84°N and across the antimeridian.

  4. Stretch: only the speed changes. With Stretch chosen, only how far the end is dragged along the line from the held end counts: the drag is taken onto that line. Every fix keeps its bearing from the held end and its range from it is multiplied by one factor, the new range of the dragged end over its old one. A straight leg stays on its line, at the new speed, on the same course; a track that turns keeps its shape, larger or smaller about the held end, and every speed changes by the same factor. A stretch never goes to nothing or past the held end: the slowest it offers is one step of speed (0.1 kn).

  5. Recorded courses and speeds go with the fixes. Each fix's recorded course and speed are carried through the same change rather than worked out again from the new positions: Debrief follows the fix's recorded course and speed for ten seconds, changes that point as a fix at that time would be changed, and takes the new course and speed from the changed fix to it. So a shear adds the leg's change of velocity to each fix's own (a fix logged at 000 at 10 kn on a leg that gains 10 kn east is now 045 at 14.1 kn), and a stretch multiplies each speed by the factor and keeps each course. On a straight steady leg every fix's course and speed become exactly the leg's new ones; on a real track the detail recorded at each fix survives instead of being replaced by the jitter of the positions. A track that records courses but not speeds, or speeds but not courses, has the missing one taken from its positions for the purpose; what it does not record stays unrecorded.

  6. Course and speed made good. What the map and the step say: the true bearing, at the first fix of what changes, of the geodesic from it to the last fix, and the range between them over the time between. For a straight steady leg these are its course and speed.

  7. The ends on the map. A track selected on its own shows a diamond beside its first and last fixes of what changes, in the theme's focus colour, drawn to the left of the way the track goes so they are clear of the pivot (often on an end) and the rotate handle (beyond the far end, on the line of a straight leg). Beside What changes, so the control stays short on a short map, its Drag the ends says what dragging one does: Shear (the default) or Stretch, which gives the diamonds a double edge. Each is named for a screen reader: BLUE ONE: shear from the end, holding the start; drag it, or use the arrow keys; BLUE ONE: stretch from the start, holding the end; drag it along the track, or use Up and Down to change speed. We chose a switch on the map over a modifier key (Shift-drag), which nobody can see and which is awkward from the keyboard, and over separate stretch handles, which would put four diamonds on a short leg; legacy Debrief, too, chose the drag first and then dragged.

  8. What the map says. Dragging an end draws the track changed as the pointer goes, the track as it was dashed beneath, and says BLUE ONE: shearing to 087.2°T 12.4 kn; end moved 1.20 nmi 045.0°T, or BLUE ONE: stretching to 12.4 kn (was 10.0 kn); with Time window, it adds that the track jumps where the window's fixes meet the rest. Letting go is one step; Escape first puts it back. What is saved is what the map said: the end's move in the analyst's length unit and its bearing, or the speed, each to the decimals shown.

  9. The step. BLUE ONE sheared: 087.2°T 12.4 kn or BLUE ONE stretched: 12.4 kn (part sheared for the fixes in a period), then Held at the start, 09:30:00Z, Was 090.0°T 10.0 kn (or Was 10.0 kn) and the period. Its provenance record holds the end held (anchor), the times of the held and dragged ends (anchor_time, dragged_time), how far and which way the dragged end went (distance, bearing), and the course and speed made good (course, speed): as asked where they were asked, worked out where they were not. Undo is replay to the step before, as for any step.

  10. The keyboard. Tab to an end. Shearing, the arrow keys move it 5 pixels (25 with Shift), as the move handle. Stretching, Up and Right make it one step of speed faster (0.1 kn, or one step of the analyst's speed decimals), Down and Left one step slower, ten with Shift. A run of presses is one step, saved once they stop, on Enter or when the keyboard moves on; Escape puts it back; presses made while the last step is saved are kept for the next. Shear and Stretch are buttons on the map, reached with Tab.

  11. The forms. Shear track… (the outline's context menu on a track; Shear… under Track, below the outline, in the playground) asks what changes, which end is held (Hold the start or Hold the end), and the course and speed it then makes good, offering what it makes good now; a speed may be typed 12.4, 12.4 kn, 6 m/s or 20 km/h, and each field says what it understood. Held at the start, the dragged end goes the speed times the period's length along the course; held at the end, Debrief finds the start from which the geodesic to the held end sets off on the course asked. Stretch track… asks what changes, which end is held, and the speed, which must be more than nothing.

  12. What is refused, and why. A shear or a stretch of fixes all at one time: BLUE ONE has fixes at only one time there, so it cannot be sheared or stretched: that needs fixes at two times. A stretch of fixes that end where they start: … so it cannot be stretched: shear it instead. A stretch to no speed. A shear, holding the end, to a course and speed that no leg ending at the held fix makes good, as can happen near a pole: … cannot make good 180.0°T at 25.0 kn and end where it does: no leg that long sets off on that course to its last fix. Hold the start instead. A change sent from a plot that has since changed is refused, as for any change (SUB-28), and a drag under way when the plot changes elsewhere is dropped and the map says so.

  13. For agents. debrief/edit_track with {"action": "shear", "anchor": "start", "distance": {"value": 1.2, "unit": "[nmi_i]"}, "bearing": {"value": 45, "unit": "deg"}} (the dragged end's move), {"action": "shear", "anchor": "end", "course": {"value": 87.2, "unit": "deg"}, "speed": {"value": 12.4, "unit": "[kn_i]"}} (the course and speed made good), or {"action": "stretch", "anchor": "start", "speed": {"value": 12.4, "unit": "[kn_i]"}}, each with a period to change only that. In VS Code, debrief.shearTrack and debrief.stretchTrack take the track and the edit, without action, instead of asking.

Not in this part: live bearing residuals while dragging, and solutions rooted in a period of bearings (the TMA module, CAP-21); shearing one leg of a multi-leg solution apart from the others.

docs.title: Cleaning tracks
docs.text:
Part B2 (14 Oct 2026). Three ways to tidy a track an analyst has imported, each one recorded step, and none done without the analyst seeing what it would do first.

  1. Jumps: found, shown, then removed. A jump is a fix the platform could not have reached in time: a GPS glitch, a mistyped position. Find and remove jumps… (the outline's menu on a track; Jumps… under Track, below the outline, in the playground) asks for a speed, offered as three times the track's median speed between fixes, and never less than 10 kn, which the analyst can change (30, 30 kn, 15 m/s). Three times the median fits the platform: a helicopter at 120 kn and a submarine at 5 kn each get a threshold far above the changes of speed they really make between fixes; the 10 kn floor stops position noise on a slow or stopped platform being called a jump. A fixed speed (60 kn, say) would miss every jump of a slow platform and flag a fast one's ordinary fixes.

    A fix is a jump when reaching it from the last good fix before it needs more than that speed (range along the geodesic over elapsed time; two fixes at one time in different places need infinite speed). Comparing with the last good fix, not simply the fix before, finds a burst of bad fixes in a row; and after a jump a fix is only back on the track when the track goes on from it, so the second of two bad fixes is found even though it is reachable over the longer time since the last good one. A jump is off the track and back: a fix the track goes on from smoothly is not one, so a real burst of speed (a sprint between drifts, far above three times the median) is not offered. Up to 5 fixes in a row can be one jump. A track that goes off and stays off longer than that, or until it ends (a ship at anchor getting under way), is not a jump, since the platform may really be there; nothing is offered. The first fix is a jump when it is far from the next two and they agree; the last likewise.

    What is found is shown first, never removed silently: each jump is ringed on the map in the theme's warning colour, the note at the top of the map says RED ONE: 3 jumps found, each faster than 30.0 kn to reach, and a list gives each one's time, position and how fast it would have been reached (09:20:00Z 37°08.456'N 075°26.932'W · 176.5 kn to reach from 09:19:00Z), all ticked. The analyst unticks any that are real (its ring goes), and Remove takes out the rest as one step: RED ONE: 3 jumps removed, with notes saying when they were (At 09:20:00Z, 09:21:00Z and 10:40:00Z), the speed (Each faster than 30.0 kn to reach) and any marked fixes that went with them. Where the track has two fixes at a jump's time (two tracks merged where they meet, say), only the one found to be the jump goes; when which it is cannot be told, nothing is removed and Debrief says so. Cancel, or closing the list, removes nothing. With none found, Debrief says so: RED ONE: no jumps found faster than 30.0 kn.

    Removing fixes keeps every series in step: positions, times, speeds, courses, depths and marked fixes lose the same fixes. A track keeps at least two fixes.

  2. Smoothing: previewed, then applied. Smooth track… (Smooth… in the playground) asks what to smooth (the whole track, or its fixes in the time window, as for a move) and over how many fixes: an odd number, 5 unless the analyst says, each fix averaged with the 2 either side of it. One method, a moving average, chosen because an analyst can say exactly what it did: each fix moves to the average position of itself and the same number of fixes either side, worked out in a flat frame centred on that fix (ranges and bearings from it, along geodesics), so it is right far north and across the antimeridian. Near the ends of what is smoothed the window narrows evenly, so the first and last fixes never move and nothing is pulled sideways. A gap in the data (more than ten times the track's median time between fixes) is treated as an end: fixes either side of it are never averaged together, so a platform that went somewhere while nothing was recorded is not pulled across the gap. Fixes outside the period stay where they are. Times never change, so the fixes stay in time order. Recorded courses and speeds are averaged over the same fixes (courses as directions, so 350° and 010° average to 000°), so they stay in step with the positions; depths are kept. Simplifying a track (dropping fixes, as Douglas-Peucker does) is a different operation, not offered: it loses fixes rather than moving them.

    Before anything changes, the track as smoothing would leave it is drawn dashed in the theme's focus colour over the track as it is, and the note says what it would do: RED ONE smoothed over 5 fixes, if applied: 236 fixes moved; the most a fix moved: 0.06 nmi, at 09:22:00Z. Apply makes it one step, RED ONE smoothed over 5 fixes (or RED ONE part smoothed…), its notes saying how many fixes moved and the most any moved, and the period. Cancel changes nothing. A track smoothing would not move (a straight, steady one) says so and records nothing.

  3. Marked fixes: a colour, a label or a comment of their own. Legacy plots let an analyst colour single fixes, label them and comment on them, and the .dpf import used to list those as not imported. Now a fix can carry any of the three:

    On the map Elsewhere Colour a dot at the fix in that colour, and the line from it to the next fix drawn in it the fix list Label the text beside the fix, as a track's name is the fix list Comment shown when pointing at the fix, with its time, position, course and speed the fix list, and the Timeline, at the fix's time, as RED ONE fix

    A fix with only a label or a comment is a ring in the track's colour, so it can be pointed at. To mark a fix: right-click it on the map (on a touch screen, press and hold it: about half a second with the finger still), or open the fix list (Fixes: colour, label or comment… on the outline's menu; Fixes… in the playground), which lists every fix of the track in time order with its time, position, course, speed and any mark, and choose one; then Colour… (the track colours, amber and yellow), Label… or Comment…. An empty label or comment, or Track's colour, takes it away. Each change is one step: RED ONE fix at 09:31:00Z coloured yellow, … labelled 'Turn 1', …: comment added (or changed, removed); a long label is shortened in the step's name and kept whole.

    A mark is kept with the track, found by its fix's time, not its place in the track (see the schema's FixMark). So it stays with its fix whatever happens to the rest: jumps removed before it, the track moved, rotated, sheared, stretched, smoothed, split (each part keeps its own marks) or merged. Where two fixes share a time, the mark is the first's; merging two tracks that meet at a time where both have a marked fix keeps the earlier track's, and the step's notes say so. Only marked fixes are listed, so a track of 10,000 fixes with three marked carries three marks, and the plot is still plain GeoJSON to other tools.

    From legacy plots. The .dpf import keeps each fix's own colour (where it differs from the track's), its label and its comment as marks. Legacy Debrief labels every fix with its time unless told otherwise; a label that only gives the fix's time (0504, 120500) is not imported, and the import says how many, since Debrief shows fixes' times itself. A label hidden in the legacy plot is imported and shown, and the import says how many. Where on the fix a legacy label went, and fix symbols and arrows, are still listed as not imported (EXT-15).

  4. What is a step, and what isn't.

    Step in the history Undone by Ctrl+Z Remove the jumps ticked Yes, one for all of them Yes Apply smoothing Yes, one Yes A fix coloured, labelled or commented on Yes, one each Yes Finding jumps; unticking one; a smoothing preview; Cancel No No Choosing a fix in the fix list No No

  5. The keyboard. Everything here has a keyboard path: the commands and their input boxes and lists in VS Code; in the playground, the buttons under Track, below the outline, the form, the list of jumps (checkboxes) and the fix list (Up and Down move along it, Enter or Space chooses a fix). Right-clicking a fix on the map, or pressing and holding it on a touch screen, is a shortcut, never the only way.

    Touch. On a tablet there is no right button, so pressing and holding a track or a marked fix does what a right-click does: after about half a second (0.55 s), the fix's menu opens where the finger is, the finger still down. It is a hold only while the finger stays within about 10 pixels of where it touched, no second finger lands, and the map does not move: a tap still selects, a finger that moves pans the map or drags a handle, and two fingers zoom. Holding a fix does not show the browser's own callout or select text on the map. Leaflet's built-in press and hold is not used: it works only where the browser says it is mobile Safari, which iPadOS often does not.

  6. Shared state and conflicts. None of these changes current time, the time window or the selection (choosing a fix in the playground's fix list selects its track). A change sent from a plot that has since moved on is refused, as any change is (SUB-28), and Debrief shows the latest; jumps found or smoothing previewed on a plot that has changed must be found or previewed again.

  7. For agents. The same through the tool service: debrief/find_jumps (feature; threshold, a speed such as {"value": 30, "unit": "[kn_i]"}, and period, if wanted) returns the threshold used, the track's median speed and the jumps (time, position, speed to reach, the fix it was reached from) and changes nothing; debrief/remove_jumps (feature, times, and the threshold for the record) removes them as one step. debrief/preview_smoothing (feature, window, period) returns the track as it would be and how far fixes would move, and changes nothing; debrief/smooth_track applies it. debrief/mark_fix (feature, time, changes: any of colour, label, comment, null or empty taking one away; colour_name for the step's name). Each change takes base as for any change. In VS Code, debrief.removeJumps takes the track and {threshold, times} (times: "all" removes every jump found; no times only finds them and rings them on the map), debrief.smoothTrack the track and {window, period, apply} (apply: false leaves the preview on the map), and debrief.markFix the track, the fix's time and the changes, instead of asking.

sequenceDiagram
    actor Analyst
    participant Host as Extension host
    participant Map
    participant Service as Tool service
    Analyst->>Host: Find and remove jumps… (threshold offered: 3 × median, at least 10 kn)
    Host->>Service: debrief/find_jumps (feature, threshold, base)
    Service-->>Host: the jumps; nothing changed
    Host->>Map: show_fixes (feature_id, fix_times, message)
    Map->>Map: ring each jump; "RED ONE: 3 jumps found…"
    Host->>Analyst: the list, all ticked
    Analyst->>Host: untick one; Remove
    Host->>Service: debrief/remove_jumps (feature, times, threshold, base)
    alt changed elsewhere since base
        Service-->>Host: CONFLICT; nothing changed
    else
        Service-->>Host: one step: "RED ONE: 2 jumps removed"
    end
    Host->>Map: show_fixes (nothing): the rings go

docs.title: Single fixes, and dead reckoning
docs.text:
Part B3 (14 Oct 2026), the last of part B. One fix moved on its own, as legacy Debrief lets an analyst drag one fix; and the legacy OTG and DR modes.

  1. Only that fix moves (over the ground; on a track plotted by dead reckoning the leg into it changes and the fixes after follow, below). As in legacy Debrief: the fix goes where the analyst puts it, along the geodesic from where it was; its time is unchanged, and the fixes either side stay where they are. Its mark (a colour, label or comment of its own) stays with it, found by its time.

  2. Its recorded course and speed are kept. A fix's course and speed are what the platform logged (its compass and log, or a GPS's velocity), not something worked out from the positions plotted, and a fix plotted in the wrong place does not change what the platform was doing. So, as for a move of the whole track, they are kept rather than worked out again. What the new position implies is said instead: the speed to reach the fix from the fix before, and the speed to go on to the fix after, each the geodesic range over the time between, so the analyst sees at once whether moving it has tidied a jump or made one. Debrief does not otherwise derive courses and speeds from positions, except where a track records none, so there is nothing else to keep in step.

  3. Picking the fix. A track selected on its own shows its move, rotate and pivot handles and its ends, as for the other operations. Zoomed in far enough that its fixes are apart on the screen (at most 60 in view, and at least 14 pixels between neighbours), each fix in view has a small ring of its own in the theme's focus colour, named for a screen reader: RED ONE: fix at 09:31:00Z; drag it, or use the arrow keys, to move this fix alone. Zoomed out, there are no rings and the note at the top of the map says Zoom in to move a single fix. The rings sit beneath the track's other handles, so where one shares a fix (the move handle, the pivot) that handle takes the pointer: drag the pivot off it, or Tab to the fix. We chose rings when zoomed in over a ring on the fix nearest the pointer: rings work the same by touch, where there is no pointer to hover, and from the keyboard; and showing them only when the fixes are apart keeps a long track from being covered in rings, or one being grabbed for its neighbour.

  4. Dragging. Drag a ring with the mouse, a finger or a pen. The track is drawn with the fix where it is being put, the track as it was dashed beneath, and the note says RED ONE fix at 09:31:00Z: moving 0.42 nmi 045.0°T; 37.2 kn from 09:30:00Z, 13.2 kn on to 09:32:00Z, adding faster than 15.0 kn, as a jump would be when either speed is above the jump threshold's default (three times the track's median speed between fixes, at least 10 kn). Letting go is one step: RED ONE fix at 09:31:00Z moved 0.42 nmi 045.0°T. Escape before letting go puts it back, and nothing is recorded. What is saved is what the note said: the distance in the analyst's length unit and the bearing, each to the decimals shown.

    09:31, moved from 09:30: faster on to 09:32

    Dashed: the track as it was. Only the fix at 09:31 moves; the speeds to reach it and to go on from it are said.

  5. The keyboard. Tab reaches each ring, after the track's other handles. The arrow keys move the fix 5 pixels, 25 with Shift; the note says the same as while dragging. A run of presses is one step, saved once they stop (under a second), on Enter or when the keyboard moves on; Escape first puts it back; presses made while the last step is saved are made as the next.

  6. The form. Move a fix… (the outline's menu on a track in VS Code; in the playground, Move… in the fix list, Fixes… under Track) lists the track's fixes, nearest current time first, and asks where the chosen fix goes, offering where it is now. The position may be typed in any notation Debrief reads (37°08.456'N 075°26.932'W, 37.141 -75.449), and the field says what it read, how far and which way that moves the fix, and the speeds it would imply: Means 37°08.556'N 075°26.932'W. RED ONE fix at 09:31:00Z: moves 0.10 nmi 000.0°T; 5.9 kn from 09:30:00Z, 4.1 kn on to 09:32:00Z. Right-clicking a ring, or pressing and holding it on a touch screen, opens the fix's menu, as on the track: colour, label, comment, and Move….

  7. The step. Named for the fix and the move: RED ONE fix at 09:31:00Z moved 0.42 nmi 045.0°T, then Now at 37°08.700'N 075°26.640'W, Speed to reach it from 09:30:00Z: 37.2 kn (was 12.0 kn), Speed on to 09:32:00Z: 13.2 kn (was 12.0 kn) and Its recorded course and speed are kept. Its provenance record holds the fix's time (fix_time), the distance and bearing (as asked, or worked out from a position typed) and the new position (longitude, latitude). Undo is replay to the step before, as for any step.

  8. Over the ground or dead reckoning (OTG and DR). Legacy Debrief plotted each track either over the ground (OTG: each fix where it was logged) or by dead reckoning (DR: the first fix where it was logged, and each fix after it placed from the one before by the course and speed logged, as a navigator plots a DR track), and asked which as each track was imported, with a checkbox Use this choice for future track imports. That worked well, since a community tends to stick with one or the other, so Debrief does the same (decision, product owner, 14 Oct 2026):

    • Importing a REP file asks, for each track, How is RED ONE plotted? (1 of 3), offering Over the ground (OTG) or Dead reckoning (DR) and, apart from that choice, as legacy had it, a box to tick: Use this choice for future track imports. In the playground that is a small form with the two choices and a check box. A VS Code list (Quick Pick) has no check box, so the box is the list's last line, showing a ticked or an empty circle and saying on or off: choosing it ticks or clears it and the list stays open, and choosing OTG or DR answers. That keeps one question per track, used the same way by keyboard, mouse or screen reader, rather than a second question after each (decision, panel review, 14 Oct 2026). Ticked, the choice applies to the file's remaining tracks and to every import after, without asking. Escape, or Cancel, imports nothing. A REP track is asked about once, whole, even where its legs were plotted differently in legacy (decision, product owner, 14 Oct 2026).
    • The import's notes say how each track is plotted (Track 'RED ONE' plotted by dead reckoning (DR).), and, when the remembered choice was used, how to change it or be asked again. They are in the plot's provenance too.
    • The remembered choice is the analyst's own setting, and can be cleared. It is three-way: ask (the default), otg or dr. In VS Code it is the setting Debrief: Track import mode (debrief.trackImportMode), and Debrief: Ask again whether imported tracks are OTG or DR sets it back to ask; in the playground, the line under Import says what is remembered, and Ask again clears it.
    • The mode is kept on the track (its plotting_mode), as content like its colour; the track's line on the map is always the positions as plotted, so other GeoJSON tools draw what Debrief draws. A track plotted by dead reckoning keeps its positions as logged beside them. Plot over the ground or by dead reckoning… (the outline's menu on a track; OTG/DR… under Track in the playground) changes it as one step: RED ONE plotted by dead reckoning, with From its first fix, at 09:30:00Z, by each fix's recorded course and speed; its positions, courses and speeds as logged are kept and the most a fix moved; or RED ONE plotted over the ground, Each fix where it was logged, with its course and speed as logged, the positions, courses and speeds as logged put back. A track that does not record both courses and speeds cannot be plotted by dead reckoning, and Debrief says why. Other changes to a track plotted by dead reckoning change where it starts, or its courses and speeds, and its positions are worked out again (below); its positions, courses and speeds as logged stay as logged, and go with their fixes when fixes are removed or the track is split or merged (tracks plotted differently are not merged, and the message says so).
    • Over the ground again, after a change made while plotted by dead reckoning, asks first (decision, product owner, 14 Oct 2026). The positions, courses and speeds as logged come back, so that change is lost; when its first fix is more than a metre from where it was logged, or a course or a speed is not as logged, Debrief says so before doing anything: RED ONE was changed while plotted by dead reckoning (its course and speed at 09:34:00Z are 055.0°T 12.0 kn, logged 045.0°T 12.0 kn). Plotted over the ground, each fix goes back where it was logged, with its course and speed as logged, and the changes made while plotted by dead reckoning are lost. Undo takes it back. (or (its first fix is 1.00 nmi from where it was logged)). Comparing courses and speeds, not positions, catches a rotation too, which keeps every fix where dead reckoning by the turned courses puts it (panel finding, 14 Oct 2026). VS Code asks in a dialog (Plot over the ground, or Cancel); the playground asks in its small form. Confirmed, it is still one step, its notes saying Changes made while plotted by dead reckoning discarded. An agent sends discard_dr_changes: true with the change; without it the service refuses (error -32003), saying why and how to go ahead.
    • A track plotted by dead reckoning is tagged DR beside its name: in the outline (VS Code's description, DR · …; a small DR in the playground's outline), and on the map, in its label and tooltips (RED ONE (DR)). Its line is drawn as any track's (decision, product owner, 14 Oct 2026).
    • Dead reckoning places each fix from the one before by that fix's recorded course and speed over the time between, along the geodesic. That is the rule legacy Debrief used: legacy saves a DR leg's worked-out positions in its plot files, and on its sample plots this puts every fix back within 0.1 m of them.
    • A legacy .dpf plot is not asked about: it says how each leg was plotted (PlotRelative). A track whose legs were all plotted by dead reckoning is imported so, with the positions legacy worked out; the plot does not hold its positions as logged, so it cannot be plotted over the ground, and the import says so (it used to say nothing).

    User state stays out of the data. The remembered choice belongs to the analyst, not the plot: it is kept in the user-settings layer (their Debrief configuration, read and written the same way by the Python services and the extension: debrief-config), never in STAC: not in a catalogue, a plot file or its history. The host (VS Code, the playground) reads it and passes the mode to the importer, and an agent passes the mode itself; the importer and the catalogue never read user state (decision, product owner, 14 Oct 2026).

  9. What is a step, and what isn't.

    Step in the history Undone by Ctrl+Z Letting go of a fix's ring Yes, one Yes A run of arrow keys on a fix's ring Yes, one for the run Yes Move a fix… (a position typed) Yes, one Yes Plot over the ground or by dead reckoning… (a track's mode changed) Yes, one Yes Choosing OTG or DR as a track is imported; remembering it; Ask again No: the import is one step, and the choice is the analyst's setting No Zooming in until the rings show; Escape during a drag; a fix put where it is No No

  10. Shared state and conflicts. Moving a fix and changing how a track is plotted change neither current time, the time window nor the selection. If the plot changes elsewhere during a drag, the drag is dropped and the map says so; a change sent from a plot that has since moved on is refused (SUB-28), as for every track operation.

  11. For agents. debrief/edit_track with {"action": "move_fix", "fix_time": "2023-06-15T09:31:00.000Z", "distance": {"value": 0.42, "unit": "[nmi_i]"}, "bearing": {"value": 45, "unit": "deg"}}, or with "position": [-75.45, 37.14] instead of the distance and bearing; and {"action": "set_plotting_mode", "plotting_mode": "dr"} (or "otg"). debrief/import_rep takes modes ("otg" or "dr" for every track, or one for each track by name) and, when the host used a remembered choice, remembered (the words saying how to change it); debrief/rep_tracks lists the tracks a REP file would import, so a host can ask. Without modes, tracks are imported over the ground and nothing is said. In VS Code, debrief.moveFix takes the track, the fix's time and {position} or {distance, bearing}; debrief.plottingMode the track and "otg" or "dr"; debrief.importRep {store, path, modes}, instead of asking.

sequenceDiagram
    actor Analyst
    participant Map
    participant Host as Extension host
    participant Service as Tool service
    Analyst->>Map: select RED ONE; zoom in
    Map->>Map: a ring on each fix in view
    Analyst->>Map: drag the ring of the fix at 09:31
    Map->>Map: only that fix moves; "moving 0.42 nmi 045.0°T; 37.2 kn from 09:30:00Z, ..."
    Analyst->>Map: let go
    Map->>Host: edit_track (feature_id, track_edit: move_fix, fix_time, distance, bearing)
    Host->>Service: debrief/edit_track (edit, base)
    Service-->>Host: one step: "RED ONE fix at 09:31:00Z moved 0.42 nmi 045.0°T"
    Host->>Map: show_plot (the ring where the fix now is)

docs.title: Editing a track plotted by dead reckoning
docs.text:
Decision, product owner, 14 Oct 2026. On a track plotted by dead reckoning the truth is its origin, where its first fix is, and each fix's course and speed: the leg from that fix to the next. Its positions are always worked out from them, each fix from the one before by that fix's course and speed over the time between, along the geodesic (above). So an edit never moves a DR track's positions on their own: it moves the origin, or it changes courses and speeds, and the positions are worked out again. A track plotted over the ground is edited as the sections above say.

  1. What each operation changes. The same handles, keys, forms and tool-service edits as over the ground; what they change:

    Operation On a track plotted by dead reckoning The step Move the whole track (drag, keys, Move track…) The origin: every fix follows, its course and speed kept RED ONE (DR) moved 1.20 nmi 045.0°T, Dead reckoning now starts from … Move the fixes in the time window The leg into the window's first fix (the course and speed of the fix before), so that fix lands where it was moved; it and every fix after follow. A window from the first fix moves the origin. RED ONE (DR) part moved …, Leg into 09:30:00Z now 056.5°T 12.1 kn (was 045.0°T 12.0 kn) Drag a single fix (keys, Move a fix…, move_fix) The leg into it, so dead reckoning puts it where it was dropped; every later fix shifts with it. The first fix dragged moves the origin. RED ONE (DR) leg into 09:43:00Z now 056.5°T 12.1 kn, Fix at 09:43:00Z moved 0.42 nmi 045.0°T, to …, Was 045.0°T 12.0 kn Rotate The angle added to the course of each fix in what turns. The whole track, or a window from its first fix, turns about the pivot: the origin turns about it too. A window that starts later turns about its own first fix, which dead reckoning places from the fix before; the pivot sits there. RED ONE (DR) rotated 12.0° clockwise, Every course turned 12.0° clockwise Stretch Each speed in what changes multiplied by one factor RED ONE (DR) stretched: 12.4 kn, Every speed multiplied by 1.073 Shear One velocity (a set and drift) added to the course and speed of each fix in what changes, found so the dragged end lands where it was dragged. On a straight leg at a steady speed every course and speed becomes the course and speed made good that the map shows; a period that turns keeps its turns, as a navigator's DR corrected for a tidal stream does. RED ONE (DR) sheared: 087.2°T 12.4 kn, Every course and speed changed by the same 0.6 kn toward 180.0°T (a set and drift) Shear or stretch, held at the end As above, the start moved (the origin, or the leg into it) and the change found so the end stays where it is as above Smooth The courses (as directions) and speeds averaged over the window, as over the ground; not the positions RED ONE (DR) smoothed over 5 fixes, Courses and speeds averaged, not positions Remove jumps Fixes with a wild logged speed (4, below) RED ONE (DR): 2 jumps removed

    An operation on the time window changes the course and speed of each fix in it, ends included: each is the leg that starts at that fix, so the leg out of the window's last fix changes too. A legacy .dpf DR leg that records no courses or speeds is edited by its positions, as over the ground.

  2. The fixes after follow on. Over the ground, changing the fixes in the time window leaves the rest where they are, so the track jumps where they meet. On a DR track each fix is placed from the one before, so the fixes after the window follow on, with no jump: that is the nature of dead reckoning. The map and the step say so: the fixes after follow on, by dead reckoning.

  3. What the map shows. While dragging, the map draws the track as dead reckoning will leave it: the later fixes, marked, and their rings follow the pointer, the track as it was dashed beneath. The note says what changes in dead-reckoning terms: RED ONE (DR) fix at 09:43:00Z: moving 0.42 nmi 045.0°T; leg into it now 056.5°T 12.1 kn (was 045.0°T 12.0 kn); the fixes after follow, adding faster than 15.0 kn, as a jump would be when the new leg is; RED ONE (DR): rotating 3.0° clockwise about …; the courses in the time window turn, and the fixes after follow on, by dead reckoning; RED ONE (DR): stretching to 12.4 kn (was 11.6 kn); every speed is scaled; RED ONE (DR): shearing to 087.2°T 12.4 kn; end moved 1.20 nmi 045.0°T; one set and drift is added to every leg. Move a fix… says the same of a position typed. What the map draws is what the tool service makes: both work it out the same way, and shared test vectors check that they agree, at mid-latitude, far north and across the antimeridian.

  4. Jumps on a DR track. On a DR track positions jump only where a logged speed is wild, so Find and remove jumps… offers the fixes whose logged speed is faster than the threshold (the same default: three times the track's median speed, at least 10 kn), in runs of at most 5 with ordinary speeds either side; a longer run, or one reaching the track's end, may be the platform really going fast, and is not offered. Each is listed as 09:20:00Z 37°08.456'N 075°26.932'W · logged 176.5 kn on to 09:21:00Z, and the note says RED ONE (DR): 1 jump found, each logged faster than 30.0 kn, so dead reckoning takes the leg from it too far. Removing one joins the legs either side of it: the fix before carries on, by its own course and speed, to the fix after. The first fix is never offered or removed (dead reckoning starts there, and removing it would start the track where its wild leg ended: drag the fix after it instead, which changes that leg), nor is the last (its speed places no fix). A wild course is not found this way, since the speed is ordinary: the track is offset from that fix on, and dragging the fix after it puts the leg right. We chose this over refusing jump removal on a DR track: a REP file's speed glitch is exactly what an analyst plotting DR needs to tidy.

  5. What is kept as logged. Edits never change the positions, courses and speeds as logged, kept beside the track since it was plotted by dead reckoning (logged_positions, logged_courses, logged_speeds). Courses and speeds changed while plotted so are content, recorded in history like any change, and undone by replay. Whether the track was changed while plotted so is told by comparing its origin, courses and speeds with those logged, so a rotation, a stretch or smoothing is noticed as well as a move; plotted over the ground again, after the warning, all three come back. Fixes removed as jumps go from the logged series too, so removing jumps alone loses nothing over the ground.

  6. Plotted by dead reckoning from the track as it is. Plotting a track by dead reckoning starts from its positions, courses and speeds as they are (over the ground, those it was logged with, or as an edit over the ground left them), keeps them as logged, and works the positions out from its first fix. We chose this over going back to older logged data: over the ground, the track's data is what was logged, so DR, then over the ground, then DR again comes back to the same track.

  7. Split and merge. Splitting keeps each part's courses, speeds and logged series; each part starts where its first fix already was, so nothing moves. Merging tracks plotted by dead reckoning makes one track with one origin: each later track follows on, by dead reckoning, from the end of the one before, so that a later edit cannot move it unseen; if that moves its fixes, the step's notes say so (By dead reckoning, BLUE TWO now follows on from BLUE ONE: the most a fix moved: 2.10 nmi, at 10:00:00Z). Tracks plotted differently are not merged, as before.

  8. For agents. The same debrief/edit_track edits; the tool service works out the dead-reckoning result, and the record of a fix dragged holds the new leg's course and speed beside what was asked. debrief/find_jumps marks a DR track's jumps "logged": true, their speed the logged speed and since the time of the fix their leg runs to.

The model, its sequence diagram and its reference implementation are written in Phase 1. Version 0 gathers the requirements it must satisfy.

docs.title: Requirements cited

docs.title: Model

docs.title: Undo
docs.text: How an analyst steps back through changes to a plot, including its colours and what is hidden, and what undo leaves alone.

docs.title: Requirements cited
docs.text: SRD Requirement SUB-21 Undo is replay to a point; tools never implement undo. SUB-19, SUB-20 Prior states are rebuilt by deterministic replay of the recorded steps; the whole history is in the plot file, protected by checksums. SUB-22 Content (data, colours, hiding) is recorded and undoable; view state, including the plot's island, is neither undoable nor recorded. NFR-10 After an unexpected exit, at most the last operation is lost. NFR-11 Saves are atomic: the plot file is always the whole plot before a change or after it.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
1. Every change is a step. An import, a tool run or an edit becomes one step in the plot's history, recording what made it, who, when, and what it changed (SUB-19, SUB-24). The History view lists the steps, newest first, and marks the current one.
  2. Undo (Ctrl+Z on the map, the outline or the History view, or the button on the History view) returns the plot to the step before. Nothing is deleted: the step undone stays in the list, marked Undone.
  3. Redo (Ctrl+Shift+Z or Ctrl+Y) brings back the next undone step. Once anything new is done, there is nothing to redo: Debrief says so rather than bringing back an older undone step. Undone steps that a new change replaced stay in the History view, on record.
  4. Go back to a step. On any step still in the plot, Go back to this step returns the plot to just after it; on an undone step, Redo up to this step brings everything back up to it. Each step shows its number, and whether it is current, undone or replaced.
  5. A new change after undoing replaces the undone steps. They stay on record, marked replaced by a later change, and can't be redone (decision, 11 Oct 2026). Nothing is ever silently lost.
  6. The import can't be undone. A plot's first step is where its history starts; to start again, import the source again.
  7. Colour and hiding are changes to the plot. Changing a track's colour (blue friendly to red enemy, say) or hiding a feature on the map, from the outline's context menu, is a step like any other: recorded with who made it, named in the History view ("Colour of BLUE ONE set to red", "Cargo 01 hidden on the map"), and undone by Ctrl+Z (decision, 12 Oct 2026). A colour or hiding change made against a plot someone else has changed since is refused, as any change is, and Debrief shows the latest (SUB-28). Hidden features never go unseen: the map shows how many are hidden, with Show all, and opening a plot with hidden features says how many. So is every annotation added, changed, restyled or deleted through its form, and the north arrow shown or removed: one step each, named (Circle 'Exclusion zone' added, Style of Circle 'Exclusion zone' changed) (decision, 13 Oct 2026; see Annotations). So is every track moved, rotated, sheared, stretched, split or merged, by its handles, its form or an agent: one step each, named for what was done (BLUE ONE moved 1.20 nmi 045.0°T, BLUE ONE sheared: 087.2°T 12.4 kn, BLUE ONE split at 09:30:00Z), with what was asked in its provenance (decision, 13 Oct 2026; see Track operations). So is cleaning a track: the jumps confirmed removed (RED ONE: 3 jumps removed), smoothing applied (RED ONE smoothed over 5 fixes) and each fix coloured, labelled or commented on (RED ONE fix at 09:31:00Z labelled 'Turn 1'), one step each; finding jumps and previewing smoothing are not steps (14 Oct 2026). So is a single fix moved (RED ONE fix at 09:31:00Z moved 0.42 nmi 045.0°T) and a track plotted by dead reckoning or over the ground again (RED ONE plotted by dead reckoning), one step each; the OTG or DR choice remembered for future imports is the analyst's setting, not a step (14 Oct 2026).
  8. The plot's island: view state that travels with the plot. Some view state is saved in the plot file, so a colleague given the plot sees it as it was left: the plot's time window, for now (one window for the whole plot, CAP-28). It sits on the plot's own details (the whole-plot feature) as its view, an island outside the history. Changing it is never a step, is never undone and is never recorded. The history ignores it: every hash and every recorded step leaves it out, so moving the window never conflicts with a change to the plot, undo and redo leave it where it is, and a plot file whose only difference is its window is never treated as edited outside Debrief. Two people changing the window at once are told, not silently overwritten: a change of view names the view it started from.
  9. What isn't undone. Current time, selection and viewport are view state: undo leaves them where they are, and they aren't recorded (SUB-22). Neither is the plot's island. Results panels stay open.
  10. After a crash. Every change rewrites the plot file whole, and the new file replaces the old one only once it is complete, so a crash leaves the plot as it was before the change in progress. Opening the plot says a save was interrupted; at most that change is lost (NFR-10, NFR-11).
  11. The history travels with the plot. The plot file holds the whole history, every step, undone and replaced ones included, so an analyst who sends a colleague the plot file sends its history. The colleague adds it to a catalogue with Add a plot file… (on the Catalogues view); one more step records where it came from, and the colleague can undo, redo and go back to any step, the sender's included (decision, 13 Oct 2026). That step changes nothing on the map, so Ctrl+Z takes it back together with the sender's last change, and redo brings both back; the History view marks both as next to undo. A step the sender had undone and not redone comes across replaced by that later step: kept on record, but it can't be redone. Source files don't travel and aren't needed: each step holds its output.
  12. Nothing is ever thrown away. All history is kept: there is no limit on steps and nothing is folded together.
  13. Checked for changes made outside Debrief. Each step carries a checksum that covers it and the step before, and the current step records the checksum of the plot's content. A history altered by hand is shown but never changed: undo, redo and every change are refused, and Debrief says what failed. Content that no longer matches its history is rebuilt from the history, with the file as found kept beside it. The island is outside every checksum, so a new time window is never mistaken for an edit.

Undo works by replay: the plot is rebuilt from the recorded outputs of the steps up to the one chosen, never by asking tools to reverse themselves (SUB-20, SUB-21). Replay rebuilds content only; the island on disk is carried over unchanged. Agents undo through the tool service's debrief/undo, debrief/redo and debrief/goto, colour and hide through debrief/set_colour and debrief/set_hidden, add, change and delete annotations through debrief/add_annotation, debrief/edit_annotation and debrief/delete_annotations, move, rotate, shear, stretch, split and merge tracks, move single fixes and change how tracks are plotted through debrief/edit_track, debrief/split_track and debrief/merge_tracks, clean them through debrief/remove_jumps, debrief/smooth_track and debrief/mark_fix, and change the view through debrief/set_view, with the same rules. Tools see a plot's content, never its island: a tool run is recorded by its selection and parameters, so it must not depend on view state outside the history; a tool that needs a time span takes it as a parameter.

sequenceDiagram
    actor Analyst
    participant Host as Extension host
    participant Service as Tool service
    participant History as Plot history
    Analyst->>Host: Undo (Ctrl+Z)
    Host->>Service: debrief/undo (plot, base it is showing)
    Service->>History: under a short lock: is base still current?
    alt changed elsewhere
        History-->>Service: Conflict
        Service-->>Host: -32001
        Host->>Host: show the latest; say nothing was undone
    else
        History->>History: replay to the step before; write the plot file whole
        Service-->>Host: new base
        Host->>Host: reload plot and History view
    end

The time controller sets the plot's window and says what is saved where. Not yet: other view state in the island, which arrives with its features. Other presentation (line styles, labels) will be content, like colour.

docs.title: Style guide
docs.text:
The style guide covers language, theme and user interface (DEV-07). It exists before the first webview or graphical feature, and pull-request review checks conformance to it (DEV-10).

Section North Star Status Language Say what an analyst would say: plain British English, glossary terms, never software jargon. Version 0 Theme Look native to VS Code; keep colour for what the data means. Skeleton; filled from Phase 1 User interface Look native to VS Code; keep colour for what the data means. Skeleton; filled from Phase 1

docs.title: Language
docs.text:
North Star: say what an analyst would say: plain British English, glossary terms, never software jargon.

Applies to every word a person reads: labels, messages, tool explanations (CAP-24), walkthroughs, blog posts and these guides. It builds on the glossary (DEV-07).

docs.title: Spelling and tone
docs.text:
• British English: colour, analyse, behaviour, centre, licence (noun), metres. Not "color", "analyze".
  • Plain and direct. Prefer the active voice and short sentences. Address the analyst as "you" in help and walkthroughs.
  • Sentence case for headings, labels and buttons: "Add annotation", not "Add Annotation".
  • Name things by what they are to an analyst, not how they are built (PRN-07, CAP-24).

docs.title: Terms
docs.text:
Use the glossary term. These replacements come up most often:

Write Not Why plot document, file, dataset A plot is the unit of analysis (SUB-05). track polyline, line feature fix point, record, row annotation shape, drawing, markup Shapes are one kind of annotation (CAP-03). catalogue repository, database, index The STAC catalogue (SUB-15); British spelling. source input file, raw file Imported sources are never modified (SUB-10). tool function, plugin, script history provenance log, audit trail In the interface. "Provenance" is fine in guides and the tool-author guide. undo to here revert to, roll back Undo is replay to a point (SUB-21). Revert alone is only the time controller's button that shows the saved time window again; it changes nothing in the plot. current time playhead, cursor Shared state (SUB-26). bearing azimuth, heading Heading is the platform's own direction.

Abbreviations analysts already use (TMA, CPA, SATC, DR, OTG, DTG, AIS) need no expansion in the interface; expand them once in help text.

docs.title: Numbers, units and times
docs.text:
Display always goes through the formatting service (SUB-04), in Python or its TypeScript twin; never format a value any other way. Rounding is half away from zero. Its defaults are this guide's defaults:

Quantity Default Example Speed knots, one decimal 12.3 kn Range and distance nautical miles, two decimals 4.25 nmi Bearing three figures, true, one decimal 045.0°T Bearing rate degrees per minute, as bearings' decimals; negative is drawing left 1.2°/min Position degrees and decimal minutes 50°20.120'N 004°07.210'W Time Zulu 09:30:05Z Date and time day month year, Zulu 11 Oct 2026 09:30:05Z Date-time group military DTG 110930Z OCT 26 Local time, if chosen offset from UTC 10:30:05 UTC+1
  • Put a space between a number and its unit (12.3 kn), but none before °.
  • Times are Zulu unless the analyst chose a display zone, which is shown as an offset from UTC (10:30:05 UTC+1), never an abbreviation such as BST. Never write a time without its zone.
  • Use the analyst's chosen units everywhere, including in tool explanations: write "the window, in the units you have chosen", not "the window in metres".

docs.title: Messages
docs.text:
Say what happened, why, and what the analyst can do next. Never blame the analyst. Never show a stack trace or an internal identifier.

Write Not Closest approach failed: NELSON and LATE do not overlap in time. Error: ValueError in closest() Spacing must be at most 100 nmi. Validation failed: maximum exceeded The plot changed while the tool was running, so its result was not saved. Run it again. Conflict (409) Imported 3 tracks, 135 fixes. Some content was not imported. Import completed with warnings
  • Counts read naturally. Write "1 plot" and "3 plots", never "1 plots".
  • Nothing is dropped silently (EXT-14). Say what wasn't done, and where to see the detail.

docs.title: Tool explanations (CAP-24)
docs.text:
Written from the first four core tools.

  • Explanation. One sentence on what the tool does, starting with a verb: "Draws rings at equal ranges around a track's position at a chosen time."
  • Judgement. Only where the result involves one. Say what to check: "Distance runs straight between fixes, so a gap in the track shortens it. Check for gaps before relying on distance run or mean speed."
  • Parameter titles. Short, sentence case, and a noun: "Spacing", "Number of rings", "Time". Each parameter's explanation says what it changes, in the analyst's units.
  • New feature names. Name them so an analyst can find them in the outline: "NELSON 1.5 nmi", "Closest approach NELSON – BLUE".

The check (DEV-10). npm run check:language, run in CI, reads the Not column of the terms table above and fails on any of those words in the extension's interface text.

docs.title: Theme
docs.text: North Star: look native to VS Code; keep colour for what the data means.

docs.title: Interface colours
docs.text:
Interface colours come only from VS Code theme tokens (--vscode-* variables), so Debrief follows the analyst's theme, including high contrast (CON-06, NFR-13). The web build supplies the same variables.

Need Token Background of a webview, and of the map's sea --vscode-editor-background Text --vscode-foreground; secondary text --vscode-descriptionForeground Selection outline on the map: dotted, never a force colour --vscode-editor-foreground Floating readouts (cursor position, scale) --vscode-editorWidget-* Hover tooltips --vscode-editorHoverWidget-* A tool's judgement --vscode-textBlockQuote-* Errors on a form --vscode-errorForeground, --vscode-inputValidation-error*

Native views (the catalogues, outline and tools views) use ThemeIcon and ThemeColor, never colours of their own.

The check (DEV-10). npm run check:theme, run in CI, fails on any hard-coded colour in the extension or its webviews, except in vscode/webview/palette.ts, which holds the data colours.

docs.title: Data colours
docs.text:
Data colours are separate from the theme and do not change with it (DEV-07). That covers track conventions such as red and blue forces, and sensor and annotation colours.

  • Tracks. A track's colour is stored with it (style.colour). On import it comes from the legacy REP symbology, so a red track stays red. Legacy's palette is kept: red #e01c3e, blue #0064bd, green #00800b, and so on (debrief_io.rep.SYMBOLOGY_COLOURS).
  • Tracks. Tracks are drawn solid, with:
  • chevrons showing the direction of travel;
  • a hollow dot at the first fix;
  • a filled, labelled dot at the latest fix, where analysts look for a track's name.

Hovering a track shows the nearest fix: time, position, course, speed, and depth where known. - Annotations. By default one amber, #c7820a, dashed and labelled, so nothing a tool draws can be mistaken for a track. That includes lines, areas and points, and everything tools draw; an area is tinted faintly (5%) so what lies inside stays clear. An analyst may give an annotation its own colour (the amber, a track colour by name, or any colour), a solid, dashed or dotted line and its width, a fill and its opacity, and its label's size and place (schema 0.0.12). An annotation drawn solid in a track's colour still has no direction ticks or end dots and is still labelled; the analyst chose it, and it is recorded. A legacy plot's annotations keep the colours and line styles legacy Debrief drew them in. Known clash: the amber is close to legacy orange (F, #ff9600), so an orange track and an annotation line differ by dash alone. - Chart furniture. The scale bar and the north arrow take the theme's text colour on the editor widget's background: they are interface, not data. - Drawing and handles. The drawing toolbar is the theme's secondary buttons, the kind being drawn a primary one. What is being drawn is sketched dashed in the annotation amber, since it will be an annotation; the handles on a selected annotation, the cross in the map's middle and the note saying what to do are the theme's focus colour on its background, so they read as interface on any theme, high contrast included. - Cleaning a track. Jumps found, and a fix chosen in the fix list, are ringed in the theme's warning colour (editorWarning.foreground, the focus colour where a theme has none): they are for the analyst to check, not data. A smoothing preview is the track as it would be, dashed, in the theme's focus colour, over the track as it is. A marked fix's own colour is a data colour (the track colours, amber and yellow, in palette.ts): its dot and the line from it to the next fix; a fix with only a label or a comment is a ring in the track's colour. Labels beside fixes are the theme's text colour with a halo of the map's background, as a track's name is. - Moving a track. A selected track's move, rotate and pivot handles, and the dashed arm from the pivot to the rotate handle, are the theme's focus colour on its background, like an annotation's handles. While a track is dragged, it is drawn moved in its own force colour, solid, over the track as it was, dashed and fainter in the same colour: the data keeps its colour, and the interface around it is the theme's. The What changes control is the theme's secondary buttons, the choice made a primary one; so is its Drag the ends choice, Shear or Stretch. The diamonds at a track's ends are the focus colour on the theme's background, the same for a shear and a stretch except that a stretch's has a double edge, so the choice is seen without colour. - Legend. The map carries a legend for these conventions. - Reference data. Land is a neutral grey-green at 35% opacity. The graticule is neutral grey. Both are chosen to sit behind the data on any theme.

All of these live in vscode/webview/palette.ts. Analysts review the palette before Phase 1 exits.

docs.title: Contrast and accessibility
docs.text:
Data colours shall remain distinguishable on light, dark and high-contrast themes (NFR-13).

  • Track labels. These take the theme's text colour, with a halo in the background colour, so they read on any theme.
  • Not yet checked. The legacy red and blue have not been measured for contrast on light themes, or for colour-blind analysts. That check comes with the analysts' review.

docs.title: User interface
docs.text: North Star: look native to VS Code; keep colour for what the data means.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
Webviews and the web build use vscrui (CON-06). They use it only through Debrief's own wrappers in vscode/webview/ui.tsx, so the library can be replaced in one place (PRN-09).

Need Wrapper vscrui A labelled field, with its explanation and any problem Field Label Text, numbers or a time TextInput TextField One of a list, including units Choice Dropdown Yes or no YesNo Checkbox A button: one primary per form, the rest secondary Action Button

Native or webview (CON-07). Lists and trees are native VS Code views: catalogues, outline, tools. They come with keyboard support, theming and accessibility for free. Webviews are for what native views can't draw: the map, forms and result tables.

docs.title: Icons
docs.text:
Codicons for interface actions; Debrief's own symbols for data.

Thing Codicon Catalogue library; read-only: lock Plot map Track pulse Annotation symbol-misc Sensor observations radio-tower Source file lock, because Debrief never changes it A tool you can run play; not for this selection: circle-slash; not available: error

The activity bar icon (vscode/media/debrief.svg) is drawn in one colour, which VS Code tints to match the theme.

docs.title: Layout across hosts
docs.text:
The same layout rules apply to native views, webviews and the web build (CON-05, CON-07).

  • Debrief's side bar. Catalogues, then the outline of the open plot, then tools: browse, inspect, act.
  • The map. It takes the main editor area. Tool forms and results open beside it, so the map stays in view while the analyst works.
  • Forms. A single column, at most about 34 characters wide for each field. The explanation comes first, then the judgement, then the fields; buttons go last, primary first.
  • Messages. Short ones go in VS Code notifications. Anything longer, such as what an import left out, goes in the Debrief output channel, opened from the notification.

docs.title: Tool-author guide
docs.text:
North Star: a scientist's first tool should take an afternoon.

This guide is for scientists writing their own analysis tools (DEV-09, OUT-06). A tool is a Python function with a declaration. Debrief builds its form from the declaration and offers it whenever it applies, without being rebuilt (TL-05, NFR-08).

This is the Phase 1 draft, written from the team's first four tools in python/debrief-tools/src/debrief_tools/core.py, which are worth reading alongside it. In Phase 5 a scientist will test the guide by building a real tool.

docs.title: A whole tool
docs.text:
from debrief_schemas import models
from debrief_tools import ToolContext, tool


@tool(
    name="lab.fix_count",
    version="0.1.0",
    title="Fix count",
    explanation="Counts the fixes in each selected track.",
    applies_to=["track"],
    min_selected=1,
    outputs=["non_spatial"],
)
def fix_count(context: ToolContext) -> models.ToolResult:
    names = [t.properties.name for t in context.selection]
    counts = [len(t.properties.times) for t in context.selection]
    return models.ToolResult(
        non_spatial=[
            models.NonSpatialResult(
                title="Fix count",
                presentation="table",
                columns=[
                    models.ResultColumn(name="Track", strings=names),
                    models.ResultColumn(name="Fixes", numbers=counts),
                ],
            )
        ]
    )

That's all a tool needs. Put it in a module and register the module (see Making Debrief find your tools). It then appears whenever an analyst selects one or more tracks.

docs.title: The declaration
docs.text:
The declaration is what Debrief, the analyst and any agent see (TL-04, TL-06). Its schema is ToolDeclaration in schemas/linkml/tools.yaml. Debrief checks it when your library loads.

Field What to write name Dotted and unique: your library's prefix, then the tool, such as lab.fix_count version Raise it when results would change. Provenance records it, so a plot says which version made each change (SUB-24). title What the analyst sees in the tool list. Sentence case, no full stop. explanation One or two sentences on what the tool does, shown on its form (CAP-24). Say what it does, not how. judgement Any judgement the result involves, and what to check afterwards. Leave it out if there's none. applies_to The feature kinds it works on: track, annotation, sensor_observations, or * for any min_selected, max_selected How many selected features it needs. Use min_selected: 0 for a tool that needs no selection. parameters The settings on its form (see below) outputs What it may return: new_features, modified_features, deleted_features, non_spatial, named_sets, state_change

Write the explanation and the judgement for an analyst, following the language section of the style guide: glossary terms, British English, no software jargon. "Draws rings at equal ranges around a track's position" is right; "Generates buffer polygons" is not.

docs.title: Which tools are offered
docs.text:
Debrief offers a tool only when every selected feature is a kind it applies to, and the number selected is within its limits (TL-08). An analyst who selects two tracks sees Closest approach. An analyst who selects a track and an annotation does not.

If a tool names a kind Debrief doesn't know, Debrief doesn't offer it, and says why in the tools list (TL-09). If your library fails to import, its tools are listed as unavailable with the error, and every other library still loads (TL-03).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Each parameter becomes a field on the form (TL-07). Debrief checks the value before your tool runs, so your tool never sees a missing or out-of-range value.

kind Form field Your tool receives number, integer Number box float or int string Text box str boolean Checkbox bool choice Drop-down of choices str quantity Number with a unit picker, for a quantity_kind of length, speed, angle, duration or angular_rate A kernel Quantity. .to("m") gives another Quantity; .to("m").value gives the number. time UTC time Epoch milliseconds (int)

Units are written as UCUM codes, the same everywhere in Debrief:

Kind Units length m, km, [nmi_i] (nautical miles), [yd_i], [ft_i] speed m/s, [kn_i] (knots), km/h angle deg, rad duration ms, s, min, h angular_rate deg/min (the analysts' standard for bearing rate), deg/s, rad/s

A range rate is a speed. A bearing rate is an angular_rate, shown in degrees per minute: 1.2°/min. In the kernel, an angle divided by a duration gives one: angle(3) / duration(2, "min") is 1.5°/min.

  • Defaults. Give one wherever there's a sensible value; it fills the form.
  • Optional parameters. Mark one optional with required: false. It reaches your tool as None when left empty.
  • Times. A time has no sensible fixed default. Make it optional and choose a time in the tool when it's None, as core.range_rings does with the start of the track.
  • Limits. minimum and maximum are in the default's unit for a quantity.

Every value is recorded in provenance, so a replay can repeat the run (SUB-19).

{
    "name": "spacing",
    "title": "Spacing",
    "explanation": "Range between one ring and the next.",
    "kind": "quantity",
    "quantity_kind": "length",
    "default": {"value": 2.0, "unit": "[nmi_i]"},
    "minimum": 0.1,
    "maximum": 100.0,
}

docs.title: Debrief data types
docs.text:
Your tool receives Debrief's own types (TL-09), generated from the schema. Each selected feature is one of:

  • Track: properties.times (UTC strings), geometry.coordinates (longitude, latitude), and optionally speeds, courses and depths. Each of these carries its unit, so convert it rather than assume it. debrief_kernel.geodesy.TrackPath.from_feature(track) gives positions at any time.
  • Annotation: a point, line or polygon, or no geometry for a note or a period.
  • Sensor observations: sensor_name, host_track_id, observation_type (such as bearing), time_range, observation_count, and a payload describing the file that holds the observations. Tools can't yet read the observations themselves; that arrives with the sensor work in Phase 4.

Use the kernel for geometry. It gives range, bearing, destination and closest approach along geodesics on WGS84 (SUB-03). Don't write your own flat-earth arithmetic: Debrief's figures must agree everywhere.

Call Gives TrackPath.from_feature(track) A path with .times_ms, .positions, .start_ms, .end_ms path.position_at(time_ms) A Position(longitude, latitude), or None outside the track range_bearing(a, b) (range, bearing) as two Quantitys, metres and degrees true range_between(a, b) Range as a Quantity destination(position, bearing, distance) The Position reached; bearing and distance are Quantitys closest_approach(path_a, path_b) .time_ms, .range, .position_a, .position_b, or None if the tracks never overlap series_values(track.properties.speeds, "[kn_i]") A speed or course series as plain numbers in the unit you ask for parse_utc(text), format_utc(ms) UTC strings to epoch milliseconds and back length(5, "[nmi_i]"), speed(...), angle(...), duration(...), angular_rate(...) A Quantity

The geometry calls are in debrief_kernel.geodesy, the time calls in debrief_kernel.time, and the quantity calls in debrief_kernel.units. For thousands of points, debrief_kernel.geodesy_arrays does the same over numpy arrays, about fifty times faster.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Return a models.ToolResult holding any of:

  • New features. Give each a fresh id with context.new_id("prefix").
  • Changed features. Same id, new content.
  • Deleted feature ids.
  • Non-spatial results. A number, a table or a graph, held column by column. Give a column with a quantity its quantity_kind and unit, so Debrief can show it in the analyst's chosen units (SUB-04).
  • Named sets.
  • A change to shared state (state_change): current time, selection or viewport. Declare state_change in outputs.

What happens next:

  1. Debrief checks the result before anything is saved. A result that isn't valid fails the run and leaves the plot unchanged.
  2. A result that changes features is saved with one provenance record, naming your tool, its version, the selection and the parameter values (SUB-18).
  3. A result that is only a number, table or graph changes nothing, so nothing is recorded.

A graph plots its first column against the others. A number is one column holding one value.

A new annotation, here a line between two positions at a time:

line = models.AnnotationFeature(
    type="Feature",
    id=context.new_id("cpa"),
    geometry=models.LineStringGeometry(
        type="LineString", coordinates=[[lon_a, lat_a], [lon_b, lat_b]]
    ),
    properties=models.AnnotationProperties(
        kind="annotation", style="shape", name="Closest approach", time=format_utc(time_ms)
    ),
)
return models.ToolResult(new_features=[line])

Use style="label" for a labelled point, "shape" for lines and areas, and "note" with geometry=None for a note at a time.

docs.title: Current time, selection and viewport
docs.text:
context.state holds the shared state when the analyst ran your tool: state.time.current and state.time.range, state.selection.feature_ids, and state.viewport.bbox as [west, south, east, north] in degrees (TL-10). It is None when the caller didn't pass it, for example an agent calling the tool service directly, so check before using it.

To move current time, select features or show an area, return a SharedStateChange. Closest approach moves current time to the moment it finds:

change = models.SharedStateChange(
    time=models.TimeState(current=when, range=context.state.time.range)
)
return models.ToolResult(non_spatial=[table], new_features=[line], state_change=change)

Current time must be inside its range, and a selection may name only features the plot will have once your result is applied, including those you add. Shared state is never recorded in provenance and can't be undone (SUB-22). A tool that only changes shared state can run on a read-only catalogue.

context.plot is the plot's content. It may include the plot's own details, a feature of kind plot with the plot's title; skip it when you walk the features, and it can never be selected. It never includes the plot's view, such as its time window: your run is recorded by its selection and parameters, so it must not depend on anything outside the plot's history. If your tool needs a period, declare a time parameter, or read context.state (SUB-22).

Don't change context.plot or the selected features. They're copies, so changing them has no effect. Return your changes instead. A result that includes something your declaration's outputs doesn't list is refused.

docs.title: When something is wrong
docs.text:
Raise an exception with a message the analyst can act on:

raise ValueError(f"{a.properties.name} and {b.properties.name} do not overlap in time")

The analyst sees "Closest approach failed: NELSON and LATE do not overlap in time". Any exception works the same way, so write its message for the analyst. The traceback goes to the tool service's log, not to the analyst.

The plot is unchanged, and Debrief and every other tool carry on (TL-03). The same holds for a tool that never returns: after two minutes it is stopped. And it holds for one that crashes the Python interpreter, because tools run in a separate worker process.

docs.title: Randomness
docs.text: If your tool uses random numbers, set uses_randomness: true. Debrief then records the seed so the run can be replayed (SUB-20). This arrives with replay in Phase 2.

docs.title: Running in the browser
docs.text:
The web build runs tools in the browser under Pyodide (CON-09). Use the Python standard library, the Debrief kernel, and libraries that Pyodide provides, such as numpy and pyproj. Don't read or write files, and don't use the network. Debrief passes your tool everything it needs.

CI runs the core tools under both CPython and Pyodide and requires identical results (spikes/pyodide).

docs.title: Making Debrief find your tools
docs.text:
Register your module under the debrief.tools entry point in your package's pyproject.toml:

[project.entry-points."debrief.tools"]
lab = "lab_tools"

Install the package into Debrief's Python environment and restart the tool service.

While you're developing, you can skip packaging. Put your module's folder on PYTHONPATH and name the module directly. From a clone of the Debrief repository:

PYTHONPATH=~/my-tools uv run python -m debrief_tools list --library lab_tools   # check your declarations load
PYTHONPATH=~/my-tools uv run python -m debrief_tools serve --library lab_tools  # serve them alongside the core tools

If a declaration is wrong, list names the tool and the parameter, and says what is allowed.

docs.title: Testing your tool
docs.text:
Test with debrief_tools.testing. try_tool runs your tool exactly as Debrief does: it checks the values, runs the tool on a copy and checks the result. A test passes only if Debrief would accept the result. sample_plot() gives a small plot to run on: NELSON and BLUE, which cross, and LATE, an hour later.

import pytest
from debrief_tools.testing import ToolRunError, sample_plot, try_tool
from lab_tools import fix_count


def test_fix_count():
    result = try_tool(fix_count, sample_plot(), ["track-nelson", "track-blue"])
    assert result.non_spatial[0].columns[1].numbers == [13, 13]


def test_fix_count_needs_a_track():
    with pytest.raises(ToolRunError, match="does not apply"):
        try_tool(fix_count, sample_plot(), [])

testing.track(...) builds a straight track of your own. python/debrief-tools/tests/test_run.py shows tools run end to end against a catalogue.
